text:
ACME/E-FIELD Flames Final Report (2019) 
 
10 April 2021 
4 
 
The research centers on the fact that electrical forces, acting on charge carriers created through 
chemi-ionization, can provide for measurement and manipulation of flames in microgravity 
environments. For example, using the drag exercised on flame ions, electric fields have 
demonstrated observable influences on flame shape, sooting behavior, burning velocity, 
extinction, and stability. The source of these influences almost certainly resides in ion wind 
effects. In microgravity, where there are no density-driven buoyant effects to contend with, ion 
winds represent an important (and perhaps the only) body force that can be applied to 
manipulate combustion systems. This project includes both academic study of electric field effects 
and aspects for practical utilization of electrical control of combustion processes. 
 
The prior laboratory experiments have shown that electrical properties of flames can be used to 
produce enhanced combustion performance by: (a) manipulating flame ions in order to change 
flame chemistry – this is generally considered a minor influence because flame ion concentration 
is typically small, but it may be critical at near-limit conditions; (b) creating a neutral wind (ion 
driven convection) locally at the flame front – this process can provide a local actuator for flame 
convection control; (c) using electric fields to affect soot formation and transport – ions and soot 
are closely linked because there are shared chemical pathways and because soot particles are 
charged by the flame ions; and (d) using electrical properties to characterize flames – e.g., there 
is a relationship between flame temperature, the carbon content of a fuel, and the ion current it

metadata.source: 22 ACME E-FIELD Flames/Reports/E-FIELD Flames Final Report.pdf
metadata.relative_path: 22 ACME E-FIELD Flames/Reports/E-FIELD Flames Final Report.pdf

text:
charged by the flame ions; and (d) using electrical properties to characterize flames – e.g., there 
is a relationship between flame temperature, the carbon content of a fuel, and the ion current it 
can produce at saturation. 
 
In 1-g, the above-mentioned processes are confounded by complex buoyancy interactions that 
cannot be unraveled. Hence, to evaluate them in detail, we propose the following experimental 
objectives for an extended microgravity environment: (A) determine the relationship between 
electric field voltage and chemi-ion current as functions of total fuel flow rate and the amount of 
inert (nitrogen) in the fuel; (B) compare the time response of the flame’s chemiluminescence and 
ion current to rapid changes in electric fields; (C) determine sooting behavior in relation to the 
electric field influences; and (D) manipulate the limit behavior of lifted flames using electric fields. 
 
The experimental approach includes a simple gas jet diffusion flame and a co-flow burner. The 
basic variations in the tests are in the burner type, the fuel type (nominally nonsooting and 
sooting), and in the level of inert dilution of the fuel to vary the flame strength. The co-flow or 
environment gas will have a nominal molar composition of 21% O2 and 79% N2. The experimental 
concept is to ground the burner to the test chamber and to install an electrically active planar 
mesh electrode downstream of the burner mouth. The potential of the mesh electrode can be 
either positive or negative, with a steady voltage or with a time varying potential (including a rapid 
step change) to examine the flame’s steady state response and time response. The data to be 
recorded include the applied voltage, the ion current, the flame broadband luminosity, the CH*

metadata.source: 22 ACME E-FIELD Flames/Reports/E-FIELD Flames Final Report.pdf
metadata.relative_path: 22 ACME E-FIELD Flames/Reports/E-FIELD Flames Final Report.pdf

text:
step change) to examine the flame’s steady state response and time response. The data to be 
recorded include the applied voltage, the ion current, the flame broadband luminosity, the CH* 
luminosity, flame images of OH* and visible light showing the flame shape as a function of electric 
potential and flame shape changes during transients in the electric field. In addition, a desired 
measurement of temperature in and near the flame will monitor the thermal field as a function 
of the electric field conditions. 
 
The data from these measurements will allow a chemical and physical understanding of flame ion 
production and information showing the potential to use these ions to electrically control the 
flame both via modification of the local chemistry near extinction limits and through changes in 
the local convection using the ion driven wind. For example, a lifted diffusion flame near its 
blowoff condition is sensitive to mixing at the flame anchor point. Therefore, electric fields acting

metadata.source: 22 ACME E-FIELD Flames/Reports/E-FIELD Flames Final Report.pdf
metadata.relative_path: 22 ACME E-FIELD Flames/Reports/E-FIELD Flames Final Report.pdf

text:
ACME/E-FIELD Flames Final Report (2019) 
 
10 April 2021 
5 
 
on near-limit flames can exert a large influence because they can affect the local mixing behavior. 
The role of electric fields on soot formation will be dramatic under conditions where the ion driven 
wind has a large influence on flow residence time (or on ion residence time, if chemical effects 
are found important) in sooting flames. 
 
Generally, the convective flows driven by electric fields acting on flame ions and those driven by 
buoyancy have been found to be of the same order of magnitude in earth gravity. In addition, 
raising the temperature often increases the ion production rate and the response to an electric 
field, but increasing temperature also increases the buoyancy effect, making it difficult, on earth, 
to separate ion wind effects from those due to buoyancy. In the zero-g environment, it will be 
possible to eliminate the buoyancy confusion and develop sufficient understanding to predict the 
response of flames to electric fields under all conditions. Extended run times are crucial for all of 
the studies because the timescales of flame property changes (which includes chemi-ionization) 
are dominated by convection (length scale/velocity) and past studies have shown that soot 
studies require high quality zero gravity timescales longer than is available in aircraft and drop 
towers. In addition, exploring instabilities and extinction behavior in near-limit flames requires 
experiments lasting tens of seconds. 
 
Overall, the goal of this zero-gravity study is to understand chemi-ionization behavior and the 
resulting ion driven winds sufficiently well so that electrical properties of flames can be used to

metadata.source: 22 ACME E-FIELD Flames/Reports/E-FIELD Flames Final Report.pdf
metadata.relative_path: 22 ACME E-FIELD Flames/Reports/E-FIELD Flames Final Report.pdf

text:
experiments lasting tens of seconds. 
 
Overall, the goal of this zero-gravity study is to understand chemi-ionization behavior and the 
resulting ion driven winds sufficiently well so that electrical properties of flames can be used to 
characterize (by monitoring ion current) and control them (via direct chemical or local convective 
influences). Electric field effects on flames have been documented for decades (even centuries), 
but flames in 1-g all include buoyancy influences that affect ion generation behavior. For flames 
near transitions and limits, buoyant influences always confound any understanding of the role of 
ion driven winds in using electric fields to characterize and manipulate flames. The proposed study 
removes this confounding influence and allows definitive measurement and analysis of the 
electric field effects on jet diffusion and co-flow flames. 
 
B. Rationale for Microgravity 
This is the ‘Justification for Extended-Duration Microgravity’ section of the experiment’s SRD from 
March 2010.  See the SRD itself for the references, etc. as they are not included in this report. 
 
As described in the Background and Overview (Section 1.1), electric field effects and buoyancy 
effects have been found to be of the same order of magnitude. In addition, in some cases, raising 
the flame temperature will increase the O atom concentration, thereby increasing the ion 
production rate and increasing the response to an electric field. At the same time, increasing 
temperature increases the buoyancy effect, making it difficult to separate ion wind effects from 
buoyancy. In the zero-g environment, it will be possible to eliminate the buoyancy confusion and 
develop sufficient understanding to predict the response of flames to electric fields under all

metadata.source: 22 ACME E-FIELD Flames/Reports/E-FIELD Flames Final Report.pdf
metadata.relative_path: 22 ACME E-FIELD Flames/Reports/E-FIELD Flames Final Report.pdf

text:
buoyancy. In the zero-g environment, it will be possible to eliminate the buoyancy confusion and 
develop sufficient understanding to predict the response of flames to electric fields under all 
conditions. For electrically driven flames, microgravity is also necessary to create conditions that 
produce symmetric flames suitable for Abel inversion and steady-state analysis. While in general 
natural convection can enhance symmetry relative to non-buoyant flames, a flame at 1-g in an 
electric wind experiences buoyancy as a disruptive influence on symmetry. Even when buoyancy 
effects can be minimized, we have found that there are periodic disturbances that disrupt the 
ideal symmetry. Highly symmetric conditions of extended microgravity are also useful for 
numerically simulating these various effects by our electrokinetic model or more comprehensively 
by others.

metadata.source: 22 ACME E-FIELD Flames/Reports/E-FIELD Flames Final Report.pdf
metadata.relative_path: 22 ACME E-FIELD Flames/Reports/E-FIELD Flames Final Report.pdf

text:
ACME/E-FIELD Flames Final Report (2019) 
 
10 April 2021 
6 
 
 
Finally, in order to fully evaluate the potential for control, it is important to examine the effects 
separately. An example of the importance of microgravity for the electric field effects studies is 
shown in Figure 2.6. This figure compares the capillary flame used for 1-g experiments (which has 
some similarities to the jet-flame companion study) when it is oriented vertically to when it is 
oriented horizontally relative to gravity. These flames behave differently in shape, size, and ion 
production demonstrating the substantial influence played by buoyancy even in the relatively 
small capillary flames. Gravity effects in the co-flow flames have been described in the SRD for 
the CLD Flame experiment, and the same influences will be important when we apply electric 
fields. Only in extended microgravity will it be possible to separate the ion driven wind effects 
from buoyant wind effects. 
 
 
Figure 2.6. Effect of orientation on combustion of 1.8 mm jet diffusion flames in 1-g. 
 
Extended run times are crucial for all of the studies because the timescales involved extend 
beyond drop tower capabilities and the microgravity quality required for symmetry and stability 
exceeds aircraft microgravity. The electric-field flame interaction tests carried out in the NASA 
Glenn 2.2 Second Drop Tower tests by Yuan and Hegde [55] showed that the flame did not appear 
to reach steady state during the 2.2 sec. drop. Furthermore, their results showed substantial 
differences in flame shape between cases where the electric field was activated half-way through 
the drop and at the beginning of the drop, again suggesting that steady state was not achieved.

metadata.source: 22 ACME E-FIELD Flames/Reports/E-FIELD Flames Final Report.pdf
metadata.relative_path: 22 ACME E-FIELD Flames/Reports/E-FIELD Flames Final Report.pdf

text:
differences in flame shape between cases where the electric field was activated half-way through 
the drop and at the beginning of the drop, again suggesting that steady state was not achieved. 
Although, we varied the range of tests performed at the Drop Tower, our research group 
encountered similar obstacles. Drop times were insufficient to achieve a steady flame after 
voltage changes in one direction. Additionally, we were unable to capture the removal of soot 
from the ignition event and the subsequent response of the flame to the electric field. 
Furthermore, testing has shown path dependence in the response time of the flame when 
subjected to step voltages of varying polarities. Properly mapping the steady-state ion current as 
a function of applied voltage requires that the flame stabilize at each applied voltage. Generally 
speaking, the timescale of flame property changes (which includes chemi-ionization) is dominated 
by convection (length scale/velocity), which is on the order of 0.1 second. In order to ensure quasi-
steady conditions of the VI characteristics for a single flame configuration with some fidelity (e.g., 
50 steps of 200 V each, with 2 seconds between steps for settling after the change), requires more 
than 100 seconds of continuous high quality microgravity. Each condition and voltage cannot be

metadata.source: 22 ACME E-FIELD Flames/Reports/E-FIELD Flames Final Report.pdf
metadata.relative_path: 22 ACME E-FIELD Flames/Reports/E-FIELD Flames Final Report.pdf

text:
ACME/E-FIELD Flames Final Report (2019) 
 
10 April 2021 
7 
 
run individually (i.e., with separate drop tests) because the 2 second settling time requires that 
the flame begin at a settled initial condition before taking another relatively small voltage step. If 
we tried to step to the initial condition, allow settling, take the base measurement, then step the 
voltage and again wait the required settling time, we would exceed 5 seconds for each test in 
nearly all cases. To run a return voltage sweep to examine hysteresis might take a further 100 
seconds. Furthermore, these times are based on 1-g results which under low ion wind conditions 
are likely to be faster than occurs in microgravity since their the convective timescales can be 
substantially smaller (under low electric field forcing conditions, for example). 
 
Understanding the electric field effects on soot is another area that requires high quality zero 
gravity timescales longer than is available in drop towers. A variety of zero gravity diffusion flame 
experience has shown that quasi-steady soot formation requires many seconds [22, 56, 57]. The 
long duration is necessary since we are exploring the relative importance of residence time 
modification of these processes in these flames. In addition, as mentioned above, instabilities and 
extinction behavior in near-limit flames generally have a stochastic character so that relatively 
long observation times are needed to quantify electric field effects. For example, lifted flames in 
electric fields can exhibit an oscillatory behavior where they alternately approach and recede from 
the burner exit until they finally reattach. Tens of seconds for this process is not unusual. Extended

metadata.source: 22 ACME E-FIELD Flames/Reports/E-FIELD Flames Final Report.pdf
metadata.relative_path: 22 ACME E-FIELD Flames/Reports/E-FIELD Flames Final Report.pdf

text:
electric fields can exhibit an oscillatory behavior where they alternately approach and recede from 
the burner exit until they finally reattach. Tens of seconds for this process is not unusual. Extended 
microgravity conditions will clarify the role of electric fields (via ion winds) on stability limits of 
flames. 
 
C. Science Objectives 
The proposed objectives text presented here is the ‘Experimental Objectives’ section of the 
experiment’s SRD from March 2010.  Although the objectives were not formally changed, the slow 
response time of the high-voltage power supplies (recommended in the ISRD) limited the ability to 
accomplish objective B.  To make up in part for this shortfall, the investigation was permitted to 
test with two different burner types (specifically gas-jet and coflow burners), where the use of 
multiple burner types was disallowed for ACME experiments to limit their scope.  Note that the 
hardware shortcoming was identified during the hardware development (and thus prior to 
spaceflight operations), but the project management decided to accept the shortcoming and 
proceed with the existing design to avoid the cost and schedule ramifications of a redesign.  
 
The ultimate objective of this experiment is to develop an understanding of the mechanisms of 
chemi-ionization in flames and to describe the interplay between convective flows driven by those 
flame ions and their generation rate. With this information it will then be possible to detect and 
control flame behavior electrically. In 1-g, laminar diffusion flames are often controlled to a large 
extent by natural convection, and particularly by the rate at which natural convection brings fresh 
oxidizer to the reaction zone. Hence, the vigor with which combustion proceeds depends on local

metadata.source: 22 ACME E-FIELD Flames/Reports/E-FIELD Flames Final Report.pdf
metadata.relative_path: 22 ACME E-FIELD Flames/Reports/E-FIELD Flames Final Report.pdf

text:
extent by natural convection, and particularly by the rate at which natural convection brings fresh 
oxidizer to the reaction zone. Hence, the vigor with which combustion proceeds depends on local 
convection. As described in Section 1, an electric field acting on flame ions produces a body force 
and convection (analogous to buoyancy) which affects the combustion process. The change in the 
combustion process can in turn affect the ion production rate, which is responsible for the body 
force. This coupled interaction is very difficult to measure, study, and understand in 1-g because 
buoyant forces (of approximately equal magnitude) interfere. In microgravity, there is no such 
complication and the body force in the flame is associated entirely with the ion-driven wind. 1-g 
experiments have demonstrated clearly that electrically driven convection can be used to modify 
the local flow field in a manner that changes combustion behavior. For example, it can stabilize 
lifted flames or force them to reattach. Electric fields have been seen to change soot formation,

metadata.source: 22 ACME E-FIELD Flames/Reports/E-FIELD Flames Final Report.pdf
metadata.relative_path: 22 ACME E-FIELD Flames/Reports/E-FIELD Flames Final Report.pdf

text:
ACME/E-FIELD Flames Final Report (2019) 
 
10 April 2021 
8 
 
though whether solely by residence time effects or their combination with chemical alterations 
has not been confirmed. In addition, ions can attach to soot particles providing them with 
enhanced mobility that can be manipulated. Furthermore, the electrical properties of flames 
provide a measure of their character. For example, non-premixed flames exhibit different 
relationships between ion production and ion wind forces than do premixed flames. The 
hydrocarbon fuel, and in particular, the carbon/hydrogen ratio, also affects these interactions. 
The goal of this project is to clarify and quantify this range of electrical effects and to then 
demonstrate the electrical manipulation of flame stability and soot in flames using the 
information obtained. 
 
To accomplish this scientific goal, there are four fundamental experimental objectives, in priority 
order, using a jet diffusion flame burner and a co-flow diffusion flame burner. The jet flame is the 
more critical configuration because it has a large 1-g data foundation and it can be more easily 
modeled as an ion and thermal source. In microgravity, however, it will be primarily driven by ion 
wind convection (no buoyant contribution and at its low fuel flow rates, the injection momentum 
dies rapidly with distance from the injector) which may limit its operating range. The co-flow flame 
allows a forced convection component to provide a wider range of flow conditions (fuel dilution 
and exit velocity) and a reproducible lifted flame for stability and soot behavior studies: 
 
A) Determine the relationship between electric field voltage and chemi-ion current as functions

metadata.source: 22 ACME E-FIELD Flames/Reports/E-FIELD Flames Final Report.pdf
metadata.relative_path: 22 ACME E-FIELD Flames/Reports/E-FIELD Flames Final Report.pdf

text:
and exit velocity) and a reproducible lifted flame for stability and soot behavior studies: 
 
A) Determine the relationship between electric field voltage and chemi-ion current as functions 
of total fuel (methane and ethylene) flow rate and the amount of inert (nitrogen) in the fuel. 
For the above determination, a low-sooting and highly sooting fuel are included, and the inert 
weakens the flame sufficiently to permit near-limit conditions at moderate flow velocities, where 
the effects of electric fields will be most acute. As shown in Figure 1.10, the resulting voltage-
current (VI) curve (also known as the voltage current characteristic -  VCC) from these experiments 
will identify the voltage and current at which the ion current first saturates, the voltage at which 
the current begins to increase beyond saturation, indicating a change in combustion behavior, 
and the voltage at which the flame extinguishes. These data can be analyzed further to provide 
the ion production per carbon atom of fuel flux which describes the flame character (i.e., diffusion 
to partially premixed), and the ion wind strength for each condition. In addition to their direct 
interpretative value for calculating ion-driven winds and body forces, these data can also be used 
in electrokinetic simulations to compute ion mobility values consistent with measured ion 
currents and to help validate the numerical simulations of other researchers that include ion 
species and electrical effects in their flame calculations.  
 
B) Obtain the time response of the flame chemiluminescence, luminosity, and the ion current to 
large step changes in voltage, as functions of total fuel (methane and ethylene) flow rate and 
amount of inert (nitrogen) added to the fuel stream.

metadata.source: 22 ACME E-FIELD Flames/Reports/E-FIELD Flames Final Report.pdf
metadata.relative_path: 22 ACME E-FIELD Flames/Reports/E-FIELD Flames Final Report.pdf

text:
B) Obtain the time response of the flame chemiluminescence, luminosity, and the ion current to 
large step changes in voltage, as functions of total fuel (methane and ethylene) flow rate and 
amount of inert (nitrogen) added to the fuel stream.  
These data provide the dynamic system behavior of the flame. This information comprises the 
time response of the flame (i.e., its surface area and luminosity) as compared to the time response 
of the ion current. These timescales can temporally separate the direct chemical effects of electric 
fields from ion diffusion and ion wind convective forcing. In addition, the system response is 
required to eventually build flame models suitable for active electrical control, assuming linear 
behavior over small ranges. 
 
C) Evaluate and manipulate sooting behavior (i.e., soot volume fraction and location of 
luminous soot) in relation to the electric field voltage and chemi-ion current as functions of total 
fuel (methane and ethylene) flow rate and amount of inert (nitrogen) added to the fuel stream.

metadata.source: 22 ACME E-FIELD Flames/Reports/E-FIELD Flames Final Report.pdf

text:
ACME/E-FIELD Flames Final Report (2019) 
 
10 April 2021 
9 
 
The interaction between soot and electric fields is very complex because it combines the direct 
influence of electric fields on the chemistry, the ion wind effects on residence time and mixing, 
and the electric forces on the charged soot particles themselves. The zero-gravity environment, 
using the combination of the jet diffusion flame and the co-flow flame provides a wide range of 
conditions where these different influences can be allowed to dominate individually. For example, 
the forced convection environment of the co-flow burner will minimize the influence of the axial 
ion-driven wind, which helps to distinguish the direct electrical effects on ion chemistry in soot 
formation. In addition to demonstrating the direct control of soot behavior by electric fields, 
separating the influences can help distinguish between neutral molecule addition mechanisms of 
soot formation and those that presume the importance of ionic species. For example, changing 
the strength and polarity of the electric field can change the availability of ion precursors, and 
electric convection can manipulate reactants’ time/temperature history. In addition, charges will 
accumulate onto soot, and the electric field can then act directly on the soot particles to change 
their residence time and path through the flame. 
 
D) Use the variation of the chemi-ion current as a function of applied voltage to characterize the 
combustion behavior of near-limit lifted flames and use the associated ion-driven wind to 
stabilize or reattach these flames. 
Because the chemi-ion current per unit flame area can be used as an indicator of flame strength,

metadata.source: 22 ACME E-FIELD Flames/Reports/E-FIELD Flames Final Report.pdf
metadata.relative_path: 22 ACME E-FIELD Flames/Reports/E-FIELD Flames Final Report.pdf

text:
combustion behavior of near-limit lifted flames and use the associated ion-driven wind to 
stabilize or reattach these flames. 
Because the chemi-ion current per unit flame area can be used as an indicator of flame strength, 
its measure (both average and fluctuating properties) with low electric field voltage can be used 
to detect flames approaching their limit condition. By adjusting the electric field, 1-g studies 
indicate that an ion driven wind can be used to reduce the liftoff height and stabilize the flame. 
This is an example of open loop electrical flame sensing, analysis, and control.

D. Science Success Criteria 
The success criteria is from the E-FIELD Flames’ portion of the ‘Success Criteria’ section of the ACME 
Integrated Science Requirements Document (ISRD, ACME-SRD-001.B) from Sept. 2013, which is 
revision B of the version prepared for the Requirements Definition Review (RDR). 
 
6.2.1. Minimum Success 
- Obtain V-I curve in quasi-steady conditions for undiluted methane fuel on either diameter of the 
gas jet burner or the co-flow burner 
- Simultaneously capture color images of flame responding to electric field during V-I sweep 
6.2.2. High Success 
All of the above plus: 
- Obtain V-I curve in quasi-steady conditions for both fuels (methane and ethylene) on one gas jet 
burner and the co-flow burner with a range of inert dilution of fuel 
- Simultaneously capture flame images during voltage sweeps to allow measurement of liftoff 
height has a function of applied voltage 
- Measure soot luminosity (radiometer measurement) as a function of applied voltage during VI 
sweeps and step changes 
- Capture color images and soot luminosity (radiometer measurement) as a function of coflow 
velocity during the Electric Field Effects on Soot experiment. 
6.2.3. Complete Success 
All of the above plus: 
- Demonstrate open loop control of flame near sooting and stability limits using ion current and 
luminosity as sensors by determining the decrease (or increase) in soot luminosity and by 
evaluating the extent to which stability limits can be extended using an electric field 
- (Desired) Obtain thermal field information for the gas jet or coflow flame to visualize ion driven 
wind 
 
 
3. Hardware Overview 
A. General Description

3. Hardware Overview 
A. General Description 
This text is from the ‘Methods / Experimental’ section of the following conference paper: 
Y.-C. Chien, J. Tinajero, D. Stocker, U. Hegde, and D. Dunn-Rankin, “Electric Field Effects on 
Flames in Microgravity on the International Space Station,” 2018 Spring Technical Meeting of 
the Central States Section of The Combustion Institute, Minneapolis, MN, 20-22 May 2018. 
See the paper itself for the references, etc. as they are not included in this report.  As a minor note, 
the sizes of some figures were adjusted in this report, but none were cropped. 
 
The E-FIELD Flames experiment is being conducted in 2018 within the ISS’ Combustion Integrated 
Rack (CIR) [15], which was launched in 2008 and used from 2009 to 2017 for a series of droplet 
combustion experiments [16].  The CIR facility is similar in size to a vending machine as can be 
seen in Figure 1.  It includes a 100-liter combustion chamber capable of operation at pressures of 
up to 300 kPa.  The chamber features a ring of 8 sapphire windows and is equipped with a set of 
reconfigurable imaging systems.  The CIR was designed with gas delivery, venting, thermal control, 
electrical power, data handling, image processing and storage, and vibration isolation to enable 
combustion research with gaseous, liquid, and solid fuels.

Figure 1: European Space Agency (ESA) astronaut Paolo Nespoli installing the chamber insert for 
the Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) in the Combustion Integrated 
Rack (CIR).  This photograph [ISS053e098207] was taken on the International Space Station (ISS) 
on 12 Oct. 2017. 
 
E-FIELD Flames is one of the six unique experiments featuring non-premixed laminar flames of 
gaseous fuels which currently make up the ACME project [17].  A modular set of hardware, 
including the critical chamber insert depicted in Figures 2 and 3, was developed to carry out the 
ACME investigations in the CIR facility.  The 0.4-m diameter ACME chamber insert provides 
common mounting for a variety of burners on the chamber axis (but only one at a time) and a 
retracting resistively-heated igniter.  The igniter has a crew-exchangeable tip and arm (to 
accommodate the various burners) and stepper-motor drive for radial positioning.  The chamber 
insert includes three mass flow controllers (visible on the far left of Figures 2-3 behind an orange 
hose and black cables) for delivering fuel, oxidizer (or an inert), and nitrogen to the burner or 
chamber.  The crew can exchange the mass flow controllers to provide appropriate accuracy for 
the desired flow ranges.  ACME’s gas delivery system enables on-orbit dilution of the gaseous fuel 
or oxidizer with nitrogen (available from the space station), but not both simultaneously.  
However, bottles of premixed fuel and oxidizer are also used, where the CIR’s standard bottle 
sizes are 1.00, 2.25, and 3.80 liters.  Fuels are stored in 1-liter bottles, while the 21/79

The E-FIELD Flames experiment is being conducted with two different burners: a simple gas-jet 
burner and a coflow burner, which can be seen in Figure 4(a).  The results discussed in this paper 
are only from the first of the experiment’s tests conducted with the coflow burner.  The stainless 
steel fuel tube in the burner has inner and outer diameter of 2.2 and 2.4 mm, respectively.  The 
coflow burner’s steel outer tube has an inner diameter of 25 mm, where the annulus outlet is a 
6.4-mm thick Hastelloy X honeycomb with 0.05-mm foil thickness and 0.81-mm cell size.  The 
coflow burner’s inner tube protrudes 3.1 mm beyond the surface of the honeycomb outlet.  While 
the inner tube is being used exclusively for fuel flow in E-FIELD Flames, valves in the ACME 
chamber insert allow the fuel, oxidizer, and nitrogen to be directed to either tube, making this 
burner capable of inverse flame testing. 
 
 
Figure 4: (a) Detail of the ACME chamber insert featuring the coflow burner (in the image 
center) used by the E-FIELD Flames experiment.  This is from a photograph [ISS053e096074] 
taken by ESA astronaut Paolo Nespoli on 12 Oct. 2017 after he installed the burner on the 
chamber insert. (b) Detail of the ACME chamber insert where the copper electrode mesh, used 
by the E-FIELD Flames experiment, can be seen above the coflow burner.  This is from a 
photograph [ISS055e001252] taken by NASA astronaut Scott Tingle on 8 March 2018 following 
his installation of the electrode mesh. 
 
In this study, a high-voltage electric field is generated between the burner and a copper electrode 
mesh located above (i.e., downstream of) the burner outlet, as can be seen in Figure 4(b).  The

his installation of the electrode mesh. 
 
In this study, a high-voltage electric field is generated between the burner and a copper electrode 
mesh located above (i.e., downstream of) the burner outlet, as can be seen in Figure 4(b).  The 
circular mesh is energized at up to 10,000 volts with either polarity, where the burner serves as 
the electrical return and the flow of flame-produced ions completes the circuit.  The ion current 
between the burner and electrode mesh is measured from the voltage drop across a known resistor 
and application of Ohm’s Law.  With and without the copper ring, the electrode mesh is 8.9 and 
8.4 cm in diameter, respectively.  The square copper weave has 7.1 wires/cm, a wire diameter of 
0.43 mm, and a 48% open area.  The mesh permits gas to pass through while also acting as an 
electrical element.  The electrode mesh is mounted 37 mm above the coflow burner tip and is 
centered on and orthogonal to the chamber axis.  The ACME chamber insert can also

closer position is being used to produce the highest field strengths. 
 
ACME’s non-imaging measurements are recorded at 125 Hz.  The measured test conditions 
include the chamber pressure and temperature, the three gas flow rates, and the electrical 
potential of the electrode mesh.  Acceleration measurements are provided by the Space 
Acceleration Measurement System (SAMS) [18], which is the primary instrument for such 
measurements on ISS and previously served that role for the space shuttle. 
 
The flame behavior is observed optically with a variety of instruments.  For most ACME 
experiments, including E-FIELD Flames, the radiant emission is measured with 6 thermopile 
detectors with a spectral range of nominally 0.2-11 microns.  Five radiometers are in a crew-
exchangeable linear array that is mounted parallel to the chamber axis.  The other detector is 
downstream and off axis from the burner.  Chemiluminescent emission is measured with a set of 
three Photomultiplier Tube (PMT) modules.  Their spectral range is 230-700 nm, i.e. in the visible 
and near ultraviolet, but two are equipped with narrow bandpass filters for measurement of OH* 
and CH* emissions, respectively.  The third PMT is equipped with a neutral density filter to prevent 
saturation, although the gain values for all three PMTs are independently and readily adjustable.  
Like many of the components, the array of PMT modules can be removed from the chamber insert 
by the crew.  In addition to their scientific value, PMT measurements are used operationally to

text:
Like many of the components, the array of PMT modules can be removed from the chamber insert 
by the crew.  In addition to their scientific value, PMT measurements are used operationally to 
detect ignition and automatically deactivate and retract the igniter.  The radiometer or PMT 
measurements can similarly be used to detect extinction and automatically end the gas flow and 
test. 
 
Imaging measurements of the flames complement the optical sensors described above.  Color 
imaging is provided by an analog color camera within the chamber and a high-definition (1360 x 
1024), 12-bit color camera mounted outside the chamber on CIR’s optical bench.  The latter is 
equipped with a motorized lens with independent control of the zoom, iris, and focus.  It has a 
filter barrel with a fused silica window (for color imaging), a blue-green BG7 Schott glass filter, 
and bandpass filters for imaging CH* and HCHO (formaldehyde) chemiluminescence.  The digital 
color camera was characterized prior to launch for color-ratio pyrometry and measurement of the 
soot volume fraction, via the techniques of [19, 20].  The camera makes soot pyrometry possible 
as well as Thin Filament Pyrometry (TFP), where the chamber insert is equipped with a translating 
array of silicon-carbide (SiC) fibers.  A 14-micron fiber array can be seen at the top of Figure 4(b).  
However, the fibers interfere with the electric field preventing the use of Thin Filament Pyrometry 
in the E-FIELD Flames experiment. 
 
Two intensified monochrome cameras mounted outside the combustion chamber are available 
for ACME use, although only one is being used by E-FIELD Flames.  It is a high-definition 
(1390x1040), 12-bit camera equipped with a filter barrel similar to that used by the digital color

(1390x1040), 12-bit camera equipped with a filter barrel similar to that used by the digital color 
camera discussed in the preceding paragraph, although it doesn’t have a blue-green filter.  The 
CH* filter has been used in the intensified photography of the E-FIELD Flames tests.  While unused 
by E-FIELD Flames, the CIR is also equipped with a high-definition (1024x1024) camera with an 
intensifier extending into the ultraviolet which can be equipped with a bandpass filter and 
corresponding optics for OH* imaging. 
 
Finally, a high-definition (1024x1024), 12-bit monochrome camera is mounted outside the 
chamber opposite a collimated light source with two fiber-coupled laser diodes emitting red light

B. Additional Details 
The preceding section described the hardware was used in the first round of E-FIELD Flames 
testing, where that was conducted with the coflow burner.  The second round was conducted 
with the 2.1-mm gas-jet burner, which was built with the same tubing as the coflow burner’s inner 
tube.  However, it is important to note that the nominal inner diameter (ID) in both cases was 
2.16 mm, i.e., approximately 2.2 mm rather than 2.1 mm.  While potentially confusing, this met 
the tolerance requirement for the 2.1-mm gas-jet burner.  Meanwhile, the nominal outer 
diameter (OD) was 2.41 mm, again for the 2.1-mm gas-jet burner and the inner tube of the coflow 
burner.  It is also important to understand that the gas-jet burner was slightly taller than the 
coflow burner, where the electrode mesh was nominally 35 and 37 mm downstream of the gas-
jet and coflow burners, respectively (based on the outlet of the inner tube in the case of the 
coflow burner).

ACME hardware in greater detail.  Meanwhile, it can be helpful to consult the ISRD, relevant

ACME hardware in greater detail.  Meanwhile, it can be helpful to consult the ISRD, relevant 
drawings, and various reports.  Some important reports include the characterization reports for 
the data camera (see ACME-RPT-010), radiometers (ACME-RPT-011), and Photomultiplier Tubes 
(PMTs, ACME-RPT-013).  Key hardware dimensions and more are confirmed in the inspection 
report (ACME-VER-001 Rev. A), while many science requirements are addressed in the ACME ERD 
Verification Report (ACME-VER-002).  In this regard, ERD stands for Engineering Requirements 
Document and many of those requirements were directly derived from the science requirements.  
Contact ACME’s Project Scientist Dennis Stocker (216-433-2166, dennis.p.stocker@nasa.gov) with 
questions or for more information. 
 
C. Hardware Shortcomings 
As previously discussed, the slow response time of the high-voltage power supplies 
(recommended in the ISRD) did not meet the requirements necessary to achieve the requested 
time response performance, and as such inhibited determination of the flame’s response time to 
rapid changes in the electric field strength. 
 
The negative and positive high-voltage power supplies were to have been coupled, as described 
for example in Appendix C of the ISRD.  However, switching between the two high-voltage power 
supplies led to excessive Electromagnetic Interference (EMI) so the power supplies were 
completely decoupled, where only one was installed at a time.  As such, testing was limited to a 
single polarity at a time. 
 
The imaging for soot volume fraction via light extinction was largely blocked by the bracket

single polarity at a time. 
 
The imaging for soot volume fraction via light extinction was largely blocked by the bracket 
holding the electrode mesh, where this was a design trade-off necessitated primarily by ACME’s 
large number of cameras and other optical instruments.  However, Prof. Marshall Long (Yale

University), who is also an ACME investigator, has an alternate technique for determining the soot 
volume fraction from ACME’s data camera (DataCam) imaging. 
 
The DataCam is unfortunately not as sensitive as had been hoped to the dim microgravity flames.  
Therefore, the imaging with that camera has typically been at a long exposure time, e.g., 0.65 s, 
even though it is a video camera capable of 30 frames per second (fps).   The principal exception 
has been when making soot pyrometry or Thin Filament Pyrometry (TFP) measurements. 
 
Between its thickness and the anti-reflection coating, the DataCam’s blue-green filter excessively 
attenuates the red light making its use undesirable.  The filter’s purpose intended was to balance 
the intensity of the three colors in flame imaging to facilitate pyrometry.  The accuracy of the 
pyrometric temperature measurements was diminished as result of this shortcoming. 
 
It is expected that lesser shortcomings will be addressed in the envisioned document describing 
the ACME hardware in greater detail than presented here. 
 
4. Preliminary Results  
A. Changed Test Plans 
To limit their scope, ACME investigations were limited to a single burner type and the E-FIELD 
Flames tests identified as required in the ISRD were with a gas-jet burner.  However, during the 
hardware development (and thus prior to spaceflight operations) it was determined that the slow 
response of the high-voltage power supplies (suggested in the ISRD) inhibited determination of 
the response time of the flame to the electric field, i.e., objective B.  To make up for that science 
loss, the experiment was permitted to conduct a portion of its tests with ACME’s coflow burner,

metadata.source: 22 ACME E-FIELD Flames/Reports/E-FIELD Flames Final Report.pdf
metadata.relative_path: 22 ACME E-FIELD Flames/Reports/E-FIELD Flames Final Report.pdf

text:
the response time of the flame to the electric field, i.e., objective B.  To make up for that science 
loss, the experiment was permitted to conduct a portion of its tests with ACME’s coflow burner, 
where such tests had been identified as desired in the ISRD.  The gas-jet burner used for the E-
FIELD Flames investigation matched the inner tube of the coflow burner.  Therefore, the tests 
conducted allowed assessment of both the coflow and jet entrainment, where tests with the 
coflow burner were carried out with and without a coflow. 
 
It had also been conceived that some tests would be conducted in which the polarity of the 
electric field was varied.  However, the switching between the two high-voltage power supplies 
led to excessive Electromagnetic Interference (EMI).  Therefore, the electrical design was altered 
such that the power supplies were completely decoupled, where only one was installed at a time.  
This avoided the excessive EMI but prevented changes of polarity within a test, as had been 
planned for the step response procedure described in Table 4.2.2 of the ISRD.  It also led to the 
need for crew to swap the power supplies to enable testing at each polarity. 
 
To be clear, these significant changes to the experiment were made prior to the spaceflight 
operations where the decisions were made by the project management to manage the budget 
and schedule.  
 
In addition to the above hardware-driven changes to the test matrix, a series of other smaller 
changes ensued as choices for more consistent scientific outcomes were sought.  All adjustments 
were based on finding more effective ways to utilize the space time experiments.  The change 
history included the following.

September 2017: Changed tests with 30% CH4 to 40% CH4 - This change occurred because ground

similar conditions.  Therefore, to ensure stable starting conditions, the slightly higher fuel 
concentration was chosen. 
 
January 2018:   Changed tests with 80% CH4 to 70% CH4 - This modification was made in order to 
better span the dilution range; we decided that changes of 30% dilution in two steps (i.e., 40%,

PMT signal strengths over the wide range of flame conditions.  Parameters were also added to 
provide more flexibility in the step response script, where independent specification of on and off 
step durations was implemented so that testing wasn’t restricted to square waves.

B. Overview of Experiment Test Operations 
The narrative description of the operations is from the ‘Methods / Experimental’ section of the 
following conference paper: 
 Y.-C. Chien, J. Tinajero, D. Stocker, U. Hegde, and D. Dunn-Rankin, “Electric Field Effects on 
Flames in Microgravity on the International Space Station,” 2018 Spring Technical Meeting of 
the Central States Section of The Combustion Institute, Minneapolis, MN, 20-22 May 2018. 
See the paper itself for the references, etc. as they are not included in this report.  As a minor note, 
the size of some figures was adjusted in this report, but none were cropped. 
 
The CIR experiments are configured, but not conducted, by the ISS crew.  Thus far, ACME’s activity 
has included the majority of the crew members, regardless of their nationalities.  Most often the 
astronauts and cosmonauts exchange gas bottles, mass flow controllers, and igniter tips.  In the 
latter case, the igniter tip exchange can occur after failure or proactively before failure when the 
crew already has changes to make changes in the interior of the insert.  While these activities may 
seem mundane, the crew play a critical role in setting up the hardware for each experiment.  As 
an extreme example, there were crew activities on 8 separate days in Sept.-Oct. 2017 to configure 
the CIR and ACME hardware for the first ACME experiment, namely the Coflow Laminar Diffusion 
Flame (CLD Flame) experiment.  In contrast, only two crew days were required to reconfigure the 
hardware for the first E-FIELD Flames tests because of the initial use of the same coflow burner.  
Planning is critical because crew activity is scheduled three weeks in advance, for which detailed

metadata.source: 22 ACME E-FIELD Flames/Reports/E-FIELD Flames Final Report.pdf
metadata.relative_path: 22 ACME E-FIELD Flames/Reports/E-FIELD Flames Final Report.pdf

text:
hardware for the first E-FIELD Flames tests because of the initial use of the same coflow burner.  
Planning is critical because crew activity is scheduled three weeks in advance, for which detailed 
procedures must be prepared and uplinked to the ISS. 
 
All CIR tests are remotely commanded from the ground from NASA’s Glenn ISS Payload Operations 
Center (GIPOC) in Cleveland, Ohio.  Typically, four to six people staff four consoles during the 
testing.  The CIR hardware is controlled from the Rack Officer (RO) and Data Management Officer 
(DMO) consoles, and the ACME hardware is controlled from the Payload Developer (PD) console.  
Two shifts of personnel are scheduled to staff these three consoles on test days because they 
typically last 14 hours with the many pre- and post-testing activities.  Given that the tests are 
remotely commanded, the operations are carried out in the day and evening in Cleveland, e.g., 
from 7 AM to 9 PM.  A day’s tests, i.e., with flames, are normally conducted in a period of 10 hours 
of less.  Tests are normally conducted on three weekdays per two weeks.  On intervening 
weekdays, the image data is downlinked and the crew often swap one or both gas bottles.  
Transferring and downlinking data from a day’s tests also requires a 2-shift day for the RO and 
DMO consoles, where it is always necessary to verify that data was downlinked without errors 
and that data is not missing.  Those two positions are also staffed to guide and oversee the crew 
activity.  As a result, the CIR consoles are normally actively staffed on four weekdays per week.  A 
team of four carry out the detailed planning for the CIR and ACME console staff, and the daily 
operational plans typically exceed 50 pages on days including testing.

metadata.source: 22 ACME E-FIELD Flames/Reports/E-FIELD Flames Final Report.pdf

team of four carry out the detailed planning for the CIR and ACME console staff, and the daily 
operational plans typically exceed 50 pages on days including testing. 
 
The science console allows for review of the analog video and non-imaging telemetry (at 1 Hz) in 
near real time but doesn’t allow for commanding.  In the case of E-FIELD Flames, arrangements 
were made so that the analog video is streamed to a secure computer at UC Irvine to allow the 
research team to participate in test operations and to recommend adjustments to the day’s 
planned parameters.  That team does not see the telemetry during the testing, but is in 
communication via phone and e-mail with their NASA research partners at the GRC ISS Payload 
Operations Center (GIPOC).  While there are many preparatory steps, the tests are ultimately 
conducted using an uploaded software script and parameter files.  In advance of the test day, the

UC Irvine science team plans the nearly 60 parameters in the voltage sweep script and specifies 
other parameters that are configured outside of the script, such as camera settings.  It is also 
possible to effectively conduct tests in a ‘manual’ mode, where parameters are changed in 
response to the analog video downlink or telemetry.  For example, the electric field potential can 
be adjusted to approach a stability or soot limit. 
 
Typically, ten E-FIELD Flames tests are conducted per test day. Despite the short test durations, 
the low rate results from several unavoidable factors.  After a test is conducted, the 125-Hz non-
imaging data is downlinked for immediate review by the science team.  A small sample of images 
are often downlinked to ensure that the camera exposures are appropriate, where the times for 
those images are typically selected based on non-imaging data to provide extreme examples.  The 
review helps to verify parameters or plan for adjustments in subsequent tests, e.g., to select the 
voltage range after determining where the ion current saturates for the given flame conditions.  
After a test is conducted, a fan circulates the chamber atmosphere after which the chamber is 
vented (to space) back to atmospheric pressure, if needed.  Midway through a day’s E-FIELD 
Flames tests, the atmosphere is circulated for 15 minutes through a filter cartridge filled with 
molecular sieves to capture any soot and adsorb at least a portion of the combustion products, 
e.g., carbon dioxide, water vapor, and incomplete combustion products.  The tests are only 
conducted when both Ku and S band communication is available through NASA’s Tracking and

metadata.source: 22 ACME E-FIELD Flames/Reports/E-FIELD Flames Final Report.pdf
metadata.relative_path: 22 ACME E-FIELD Flames/Reports/E-FIELD Flames Final Report.pdf

text:
e.g., carbon dioxide, water vapor, and incomplete combustion products.  The tests are only 
conducted when both Ku and S band communication is available through NASA’s Tracking and 
Data Relay Satellite (TDRS) System.  Depending on the various orbits, there are periodic 
communication outages with a loss of signal (LOS) that can be a short handover (from one satellite 
to another) or can last as long as 30 minutes. 
 
A variety of constraints limit the number of tests that can be performed, both overall and on a 
daily basis.  The next combustion experiments in the CIR will feature solid fuels and focus on flame 
spread and material flammability.  That follow-on plan limits the duration of ACME operations, 
where each ACME experiment is allotted four months for testing.  Although it requires additional 
crew time, these allotments are split into two rounds so that the investigators have a break from 
testing for careful review of the early results so that they can maximize the scientific outcome of 
their second round.  This paper reports on early results from the first round of E-FIELD Flames. 
 
While nitrogen is available from the space station, the combustion testing is limited by the 
available gas bottles that were and are launched to support the tests.  For E-FIELD Flames and 
most of ACME’s experiments, the test matrices used to plan those gas resources were established 
in 2010.  At that time, NASA limited the scope of the ACME tests matrices with the intent of 
focused experiments with limited objectives rather than comprehensive experiments.  As such, 
the general target was 50 tests per experiment.  For most ACME experiments, the limiting gas 
constraint is the oxygen/nitrogen bottles used to fill the chamber.  This resource constraint is

metadata.source: 22 ACME E-FIELD Flames/Reports/E-FIELD Flames Final Report.pdf
metadata.relative_path: 22 ACME E-FIELD Flames/Reports/E-FIELD Flames Final Report.pdf

text:
the general target was 50 tests per experiment.  For most ACME experiments, the limiting gas 
constraint is the oxygen/nitrogen bottles used to fill the chamber.  This resource constraint is 
exacerbated by the CIR because it is equipped with a pair of redundant safety timers to limit the 
fuel that can flow into the combustion chamber (where the timers can be set for the oxidizer flow 
in the case of inverse flame testing).  The timers can only be reset by venting the combustion 
chamber.  Therefore, the timer limit combined with other constraints effectively corresponds to 
the day’s maximum flow time for the fuel (or more generally, the limiting reactant).  For E-FIELD 
Flames, the safety timers are set to the maximum value of 999 seconds, which corresponds to the 
10 tests typically completed per day. 
 
Another constraint is the available time in a day, where the console personnel and ISS resources, 
such as the video downlink, are planned for a limited number of hours.  When necessary for the

10 April 2021 
21 
 
research, NASA does have continuous 24-hour/day operations for some non-CIR experiments.  
But as discussed, the ACME tests are typically two minutes or less in duration, so the testing is 
almost always limited to the planned durations. 
 
Data limits are yet another constraint, where the on-orbit hardware can store a limited amount 
of data.  More importantly, 127,000 MB is the most that can be reasonably managed in a two-
shift transfer and downlink day.  Therefore, tests days are limited to this amount of data, where 
image data from select cameras is often archived at reduced rates to mitigate this challenge.  
Nonetheless, the limit sometimes forces decisions to abandon recorded images. 
 
This detailed description of operations and hardware provides the context under which the ACME 
experiments are conducted.  Their complexity makes the flame conditions seem trivial in 
comparison.  It is a simple coflow flame, with just a small jet of fuel surrounded by a weak coflow 
of ‘air’ which also fills the chamber, but where tests are also conducted with no coflow.  A test 
includes starting the gas flows to prime the system, energizing the igniter to initiate a flame, 
retracting the igniter, and allowing the flame to steady slightly before energizing the electric field 
to its initial value.  The flame is again allowed to steady before beginning a voltage sweep over a 
specified range with steps or smooth ramps of specified voltage changes and durations.  The 
sweep can be in one direction or can include cycles of sweeps.  After each test, a duplicate field 
sweep is made to ensure that there are no current leaks, i.e., other than the ion current through 
the flame.

sweep can be in one direction or can include cycles of sweeps.  After each test, a duplicate field 
sweep is made to ensure that there are no current leaks, i.e., other than the ion current through 
the flame. 
 
The first phase tests in E-FIELD Flames employ the coflow burner geometry shown in Figure 4, 
with the fuel tube extending slightly above the burner surface.  The results shown in this paper 
are for tests conducted with 100% methane in a chamber atmosphere and coflow (when used) of 
synthetic ‘air’ (i.e., 21/79 oxygen/nitrogen by volume) at a nominal pressure of 100 kPa.  The mesh 
is held at a negative potential relative to the burner in these tests.  The sweeps shown in this 
paper extend to at least -7 kV, where the voltage is increased in small steps (e.g., of 100 V) lasting 
1-2 seconds.  The details of the voltage changes can be seen in the resulting plots.

C. Summary of Preliminary Results 
The following text is the abstract from a 2019 conference paper on early results from the first 
round of testing: 
Y.-C., Chien, J. Tinajero, D. Stocker, D., U. Hegde, U. and D. Dunn-Rankin, “Ion Current and 
Flame Changes with Electric Fields in Microgravity,” 11th U.S. National Combustion Meeting 
2019, Pasadena, CA, 24-27 March 2019. 
 
This work presents changes in reaction zone shape and location, as well as ion currents obtained 
after applying an electric field onto a diffusion flame with fuel dilution in the International Space 
Station (ISS). As one of the projects of Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments 
(ACME), the E-FIELD Flames experiments were initiated in March and completed in November of 
2018 with a series of flame studies on the coflow burner and the jet burner within the Combustion 
Integrated Rack (CIR). The coflow burner, presented in this paper, consists of a small central fuel 
jet and a concentric outer ring flowing with synthetic air. The research examines fundamental 
hydrocarbon flame behaviors driven by the chemi-ion response during the combustion process. 
The experiment is conducted by applying high voltage onto a copper mesh situated 37 mm above 
the burner tip, where measurements include images and ion currents over a range of electric field 
strengths and time histories depending on the region of interest (e.g., near the saturation 
transition). This paper specially investigates the flame behavior while flowing different 
methane/nitrogen mixture compositions. Among other effects, the results show that the electric 
field can stabilize the microgravity diffusion flame at very high dilution conditions, especially when

metadata.source: 22 ACME E-FIELD Flames/Reports/E-FIELD Flames Final Report.pdf
metadata.relative_path: 22 ACME E-FIELD Flames/Reports/E-FIELD Flames Final Report.pdf

text:
methane/nitrogen mixture compositions. Among other effects, the results show that the electric 
field can stabilize the microgravity diffusion flame at very high dilution conditions, especially when 
there is no coflowing air. 
 
The preliminary results are discussed in greater detail in sections based on the burner 
configuration (coflow burner and jet burner), fuel (methane and ethylene), and dilution levels 
tested.  First presented are the results from the methane flames with the coflow burner and then 
with the jet burner.  Then, the ethylene flame results are presented.  Before providing the results, 
it is important to clarify the terminology of polarity and field direction adopted for this system. 
 
Field direction and polarities 
The electric field is established between the two electrodes, burner and mesh, which are 
connected separately with positive and negative polarity, as the test requires.  Because this 
research has no gravitationally relevant direction, any orientation can serve as the spatial 
reference coordinate.  The vast majority of research in electric field related combustion study is 
conducted at earth gravity, where the buoyancy is one of the key properties considered and 
repeatedly discussed.  In microgravity, a facing upright burner is equivalent to one facing upside 
down (or even sideways) scientifically because the buoyancy/gravitation force is zero.  To 
maintain the concept where the nominal field strength coincides with the direction of an ion 
driven wind that results from positive ions flowing from high to low potential, the positive field 
direction aligns with the fluid flow direction (where the jet flows) from burner to mesh, as positive

metadata.source: 22 ACME E-FIELD Flames/Reports/E-FIELD Flames Final Report.pdf
metadata.relative_path: 22 ACME E-FIELD Flames/Reports/E-FIELD Flames Final Report.pdf

text:
driven wind that results from positive ions flowing from high to low potential, the positive field 
direction aligns with the fluid flow direction (where the jet flows) from burner to mesh, as positive 
ions repel from the burner (Enominal= -V/d); a negative electric field is the opposite direction from 
mesh to burner, and the positive ions move toward the burner, as indicated in Figure 7.

The first set of results show the voltage-current (V-I) curve for flames in microgravity.  The curves 
are qualitatively similar, with a parabolic increase in ion current with increasing nominal field 
strength, up to a peak.  Following the peak, increasing the voltage creates a distinct decrease in 
ion current, towards a saturation plateau, where the ion current remains constant with increasing 
field strength.  Although the plateau is not apparent in Figure 8, it is clearly seen in all cases when 
a sufficient field strength is applied (e.g., Fig. 9), where the sufficient field strength depends on 
the fuel flow rate and coflow.  In all the curves, the jagged features are spikes following a voltage 
step change that are mostly associated with the transient capacitance of the system when rapid 
steps are requested.  These overshoots notwithstanding, the V-I curves follow smooth and 
reproducible trajectories. 
 
For comparison, the equivalent V-I curves for 1-g flames with the same burner configuration with 
no coflow are shown Figure 10 [J. Tinajero, dissertation, 2015].  The results are too recent to allow 
a detailed analysis and discussion, but some significant observations from these results and the 
comparison follow. 
 
1. The ion current peaks at approximately the same field strength for both velocities in 1-g while 
in microgravity the ion current peak for a lower fuel velocity occurs at a lower field strength, 
where the field strength at the peak current seems to scale linearly with the fuel velocity.

text:
in microgravity the ion current peak for a lower fuel velocity occurs at a lower field strength, 
where the field strength at the peak current seems to scale linearly with the fuel velocity. 
   
2. In microgravity, the ion current does not smoothly increase to saturation nor does it show a 
gentle peak with a mild decrease as is seen in the normal gravity results.  Instead, there is a distinct 
peak in the ion current with a severe decrease to a saturation condition.  That is, the microgravity 
saturation is not the maximum ion current observed.  This difference is more dramatic when there 
is no coflow, which suggests that entrainment plays an important role whether caused by 
buoyancy or a forced coflow.

To help clarify some of the ion current behaviors, Figures 11-12 show representative flame images 
from the color digital camera at different field strengths for the four cases presented.  The flame 
geometry changes very little in the presence of a weak electric field.  With a weak coflow, these 
low-momentum microgravity flames form nominally spherical shapes with a weak (or no) electric 
field, as seen in the leftmost images.  But in the absence of the coflow, the flame broadens to 
reach more oxygen and lifts from the burner. 
 
From the middle three images, we can see that as the electric field increases, the ion driven wind 
pulls upwards on the flame and entrains oxidizer into it.  This increases the intensity of the 
reaction producing more ions per unit surface area and increasing the overall ion current.  At field 
strengths greater than that resulting in the peak ion current, voltage increases cause an expansion 
of the flame and a decrease in reaction intensity, which drops the overall ion current.  This does 
not happen in normal gravity because the buoyancy dominates the flame shape.  The cause for 
the expansion in the flame size at higher voltage is not yet clearly understood, though it may be 
that there is a stronger radial ion flux at higher voltages.  Regardless, the behavior of a peak ion 
current is different than that seen at normal gravity.

Images of a methane jet flame at 19 cm/s for positive and negative field strengths, are shown in 
Fig. 17 and Fig. 19, respectively. The very first image of each condition, e.g., 0.05 kV/cm, 
demonstrates the initial voltage stage before the voltage sweep experiment.  The jet flames are 
relatively more stable initially and less stable under high voltage than the previously reported jet 
flames using a coflow burner with no coflow.  As the positive field is applied to the jet, the flame 
becomes compact in width and height. The immediate change observed is the bright soot 
aggregating around the flame tip.  With an increase of electric field strength, the flame shrinks 
and the soot is less distributed at the tip.  The voltage is swept at 350 volts per step and held at 
each voltage for two seconds. The ion current is sampled at 125 Hz (like the rest of the non-
imaging data) and the monitored current fluctuation at the same voltage step is shown in the

text:
each voltage for two seconds. The ion current is sampled at 125 Hz (like the rest of the non-
imaging data) and the monitored current fluctuation at the same voltage step is shown in the 
graph.  The ion current to electric field strength (V-I) graph is plotted for 24 and 19 cm/s flow 
velocity in Fig. 18, and the current is initially increasing parabolically with the voltage applied.  The 
ion current corresponds to the flame appearance in that the current increases and reaches a peak 
at the most compact flame, e.g. 1.28 kV/cm for 19 cm/s (Fig. 18b) where the soot is almost gone 
(Fig. 17).  The flame base starts rising slightly around the current peak 1.28 kV/cm and lifts higher, 
with one side of the reaction wing attached to the tube, as the electric field increases further.  The 
flame is not always lifted at the same side/edge of the burner tube, therefore, the attached 
reaction wing sometimes rotates along the tube edge with approximately the same lift angle 
under the same electric field strength but even the lifted edge flame remains relatively stable.  
With further electric field increase, the flame starts fluctuating and a distinct dancing 
phenomenon can be seen from the I-V curve where the ion current oscillates widely at the same 
field strength; the fluctuation is crossing more than 3.5 A  (between ~ 1.2 to 5 A) and reaching 
5.0 A for 24 cm/s.  Similarly, this oscillation at the same voltage is observed for 19 cm/s with the 
ion current spanning around 2.5 A (~ 1.4 to 4 A) and reaching 4.0 A; the flame images are 
shown as 1.76 and 2.04 kV/cm in Fig. 17. These very high peak values may represent an incipient 
corona or discharge event.  The combustion extinguishes with the oscillation at 1.84 kV/cm for 24 
cm/s and 2.04 kV/cm for 19 cm/s.

evaluation of this soot sparking is underway.

D. Surprises and New Discoveries 
We expect many more discoveries to arise as we sort through the detailed data sets, but the initial 
surprises and discoveries include: 
 
(1) The behavior of the V-I curve is distinctly different in microgravity as compared to 1-g flames, 
where in microgravity there is not a distinctive saturation ion current plateau but rather the 
flames exhibit a distinct peak ion current that corresponds to the most compact flame.  These 
results show that buoyancy driven flows are an important influence on 1-g flames even when an 
electric field is applied. 
 
(2) When soot is present in a flame, electric fields create a wide range of unpredictable behaviors 
that include elimination of the soot through what appears to be enhanced mixing for combustion, 
showers of luminous particles that are likely to be incandescent soot agglomerates, and unstable 
dancing flames.  Sooting is far more significant in flames in microgravity than is seen in similar 
conditions with 1-g flames. 
 
(3) There are clear correlations between flame luminosity, combustion intensity, and ion current.  
The results suggest that the most robust burning also produces the highest ion current, even 
though the flame is most compact. 
 
(4) The very weak low fuel concentration flames were stabilized at ignition with very small electric 
fields, where without the fields the flames would quickly quench.  This stabilizing feature of

metadata.source: 22 ACME E-FIELD Flames/Reports/E-FIELD Flames Final Report.pdf
metadata.relative_path: 22 ACME E-FIELD Flames/Reports/E-FIELD Flames Final Report.pdf

text:
though the flame is most compact. 
 
(4) The very weak low fuel concentration flames were stabilized at ignition with very small electric 
fields, where without the fields the flames would quickly quench.  This stabilizing feature of 
electric fields for weak zero gravity flames was a surprise, and it suggests that electric fields may 
be a good tool for approximating buoyancy body forces at partial gravity. 
 
(5) Jet flames under the influence of the electric field were unstable at high field strengths, and 
these flames experienced corona and then arc discharges due to the large field concentration 
near the jet burner tip.  The flame behavior was dramatic but difficult to characterize, suggesting 
a spatially- and time-varying field/flame interaction.

ACME/E-FIELD Flames Final Report (2019) 
 
10 April 2021 
38 
 
E. Accomplishment of Approved Objectives 
All major science objectives were accomplished.  As identified below, objectives A, B, C, and D, 
were completed with differing degrees of success. 
 
A) Determine the relationship between electric field voltage and chemi-ion current as functions 
of total fuel (methane and ethylene) flow rate and the amount of inert (nitrogen) in the fuel. 
This was accomplished through the collection of V-I curves at all experiment conditions.  This 
objective was completed with great success. 
 
B) Obtain the time response of the flame chemiluminescence, luminosity, and the ion current to 
large step changes in voltage, as functions of total fuel (methane and ethylene) flow rate and 
amount of inert (nitrogen) added to the fuel stream. 
Although the power supplies were not capable of rapid downward voltage changes, the upward 
steps were sufficiently fast to permit the time response evaluation.  In microgravity, the 
preliminary results suggest that the time response is faster than is seen in 1-g suggesting that the 
changes in the buoyancy driven flows play a role in the time response of these flames on earth.  
The scientific understanding associated with this objective was sufficient. 
 
C) Evaluate and manipulate sooting behavior (i.e., soot volume fraction and location of 
luminous soot) in relation to the electric field voltage and chemi-ion current as functions of total 
fuel (methane and ethylene) flow rate and amount of inert (nitrogen) added to the fuel stream. 
This objective was only partially completed because the key soot volume fraction instrument was 
unavailable to the experiment because of the obscuration of the High-Bitdepth Multispectral

metadata.source: 22 ACME E-FIELD Flames/Reports/E-FIELD Flames Final Report.pdf
metadata.relative_path: 22 ACME E-FIELD Flames/Reports/E-FIELD Flames Final Report.pdf

text:
This objective was only partially completed because the key soot volume fraction instrument was 
unavailable to the experiment because of the obscuration of the High-Bitdepth Multispectral 
(HiBMs) camera by the bracket holding the electrode mesh.  The location of the luminous soot 
was identifiable, however, so the qualitative results were completed.  There is, however, the 
potential to use additional calibration of the ACME color camera and the associated pyrometry 
and total luminosity to provide the temperature and soot volume fraction from the images that 
were collected.  This objective was met sufficiently. 
 
D) Use the variation of the chemi-ion current as a function of applied voltage to characterize the 
combustion behavior of near-limit lifted flames and use the associated ion-driven wind to 
stabilize or reattach these flames. 
Both aspects of flames mentioned in the objective were determined.  As mentioned above, the 
electric field was definitely successful in stabilizing flames that would otherwise quench after 
ignition or not burn stably.  There was not an opportunity to produce true near-limit lifted flames, 
but the effect of the ion-driven wind for generating more intense combustion and compact flames 
was clearly demonstrated.  This objective was met sufficiently.  
 
The formal success criteria were presented in Section 2.D.  As can be seen from the science 
objectives completed, the project definitely met the high success criteria and partially met the 
complete success criteria.  Complete success was only missed because, as described under the 
objectives, only some time response data was obtained, and there were specific cases where the 
ion-driven wind helped stabilize flames that would otherwise be difficult to achieve a sustained

text:
objectives, only some time response data was obtained, and there were specific cases where the 
ion-driven wind helped stabilize flames that would otherwise be difficult to achieve a sustained 
ignition.  The electric field was also able to blow out flames under some conditions.  The response 
time of the power supplies, and the inability to switch polarity during a single experiment

text:
ACME/E-FIELD Flames Final Report (2019) 
 
10 April 2021 
39 
 
(different power supplies were needed) made it impossible to fully test the open loop control of 
the flame. 
 
We also had a desired objective of imaging the thermal field around the flame.  This information 
would be very valuable for providing direct imaging of the ion-driven hot gas plume.  Schlieren or 
shadowgraph imaging was not available to the ISS experiment.  One alternative would be to run 
a limited number of long-duration drop tests using a schlieren rig and an equivalent electric field 
burner, but the path to this outcome is not yet formally defined. 
 
F. Additional Objectives Achieved 
As we became more familiar with the conditions that provided the most impactful data, we 
reconstructed some test cases to provide more comprehensive matching of fundamental 
conditions.  For example, it is known that flames of similar character (i.e., temperature and 
intensity) have saturation ion currents that scale with the input carbon to the flame.  This is 
because the dominant chemical pathway to the key ion species includes HCO+.  Hence, to examine 
this feature of flames under electric field influence, we ran additional conditions with matching 
input carbon content. 
 
Matching carbon content with higher or lower flow rates: In addition to the core objectives 
achieved, experiments were run to match the carbon content of flames as a test for the role of 
fuel carbon in the ion-current peak production.  Classical theory shows that ion current scales with 
carbon content for premixed flames, and some 1-g data shows similar trends for diffusion flames, 
but no one had determined if the concept held for zero-g flames.

metadata.source: 22 ACME E-FIELD Flames/Reports/E-FIELD Flames Final Report.pdf
metadata.relative_path: 22 ACME E-FIELD Flames/Reports/E-FIELD Flames Final Report.pdf

text:
carbon content for premixed flames, and some 1-g data shows similar trends for diffusion flames, 
but no one had determined if the concept held for zero-g flames. 
 
Flame response hysteresis: We also obtained data for flames where the electric field was ramped 
up and down to determine any effects of hysteresis in the ion current or flame response.  This 
was an additional objective achieved.   
 
G. Impacts, Benefits, and Products 
The impact of this work is, as the original objectives identified, the delivery of a unique data set 
of chemi-ion behavior in flames under sufficiently stable and symmetric conditions that models 
and theories can be evaluated against the results.  As an example, the very distinctive shape of 
the V-I curve in microgravity, when matched in models, will give a very good indication that the 
feedback between ion driven wind and changes in flame shape and burning behavior that then 
further change the ion current is captured accurately. 
 
These results have already garnered the interest of other groups working on electric field effects 
on flames.  
 
The use of electric field effects on flames can be as sensor (variations of ion current as associated 
with combustion behavior) or actuator (ion-driven wind changes the flame shape and 
characteristics).  This work, as was originally planned, provides quantitative evaluation of the 
sensing and response potential of electric fields in combustion.  The applications can include the 
control of flames.
