ACME/E-FIELD Flames Final Report (2019) 
 
10 April 2021 
40 
 
Follow-On Experiments  
We hope to have a third round of testing so that we can concentrate on flames in the coflow 
burner configuration that we found to be the more useful and symmetric than those with the jet 
burner.  It is likely that the more uniform electric field is responsible for this observation.  
 
As noted above, useful results regarding the flame response time were obtained despite the slow 
response time of the power supply time through tests with fast upward voltage steps in some 
configurations.  The step response is not as comprehensive as we would like, however, to confirm 
the links between the ion driven wind as actuator and sensor. 
 
For objective D, we obtained very interesting information about flame stabilization and 
destabilization using electric fields but not in the manner we expected.  Rather the destabilizing 
influence of the field producing fluctuations in the flame was more pronounced a phenomenon 
than we had seen when buoyancy was also part of the body force involved.  We did not get to 
limit flames except that we showed clearly how in microgravity a flame can be stabilized with a 
small field rather than simply expanding and extinguishing.  So that is some information again at 
the limit.  We can discover more by concentrating on very low field strengths. 
 
The outcomes of the first two rounds justify further testing because the results were so successful.  
The success showed how perfectly the E-FIELD Flames experiment fits the capabilities and 
limitations of the CIR.  It is a configuration that can use the imaging capabilities at their current 
performance effectively.  The experiments manipulate flames between quasi-steady behaviors in

metadata.source: 22 ACME E-FIELD Flames/Reports/E-FIELD Flames Final Report.pdf
metadata.relative_path: 22 ACME E-FIELD Flames/Reports/E-FIELD Flames Final Report.pdf

text:
limitations of the CIR.  It is a configuration that can use the imaging capabilities at their current 
performance effectively.  The experiments manipulate flames between quasi-steady behaviors in 
microgravity rather than passively observing non-steady flames evolving.  The first rounds of 
testing spanned the experimental configuration space in terms of gases, flow rates, field ranges, 
and burner types.  These spanning experiments mapped the phenomena but did not allow a deep 
dive into the conditions that showed the most dramatic changes of flame character with changes 
in electric field strength.  In addition, excessive amounts of soot made unraveling some of the gas 
phase ion chemistry more complicated in the pure fuel cases, so we can now concentrate on 
moderate sooting cases.  In general, the bonus tests let us go back to the known "best case" 
situations and resolve the processes (e.g., flame shape, luminosity, soot formation and 
disappearance, ion current).  That is the matrix we proposed.  
 
It is not within the scope of the current work, but we continue to advocate for a Schlieren imaging 
capability in zero-g combustion systems.  The ability to image hot gas flows would benefit a range 
of experiments and would be particularly useful for the flames in electric field situations because 
alternative methods for determining flows would not be possible in the high field environments.  
It may be that the 5-second drop facility is appropriate for many of these companion tests.

Electric-Field Effects on Laminar Diffusion Flames 
E-FIELD Flames is one of several independent experiments that are part of the ACME project, 
which uses a single modular set of hardware to carry out studies of flames burning gaseous fuels 
in the ISS’ Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR). 
 
Prepared by the PI team and Dennis Stocker (dennis.p.stocker@nasa.gov), the ACME Project 
Scientist, who is the primary contact for E-FIELD Flames and ACME information.

I.  Introduction 
The Electric-Field Effects on Laminar Diffusion Flames (E-FIELD Flames) experiment is conducted 
in the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) on the International Space Station, as part of the 
Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) project.  In this experiment, an 
electric field with voltages as high as 10,000 volts is established between the burner and a flat, 
circular mesh electrode suspended above (i.e., downstream of) the burner.  The motion of the

metadata.source: 22 ACME E-FIELD Flames/Reports/E-FIELD Flames Final Report.pdf
metadata.relative_path: 22 ACME E-FIELD Flames/Reports/E-FIELD Flames Final Report.pdf

text:
electric field with voltages as high as 10,000 volts is established between the burner and a flat, 
circular mesh electrode suspended above (i.e., downstream of) the burner.  The motion of the 
charged ions, which are naturally produced within the flame, are strongly affected by a strong 
electric field.  The resulting ion-driven wind can dramatically influence the stability and sooting 
behavior of the flame.  Measurements are made of electric-field strength, the ion current passing 
through the flame, and flame characteristics such as the size, structure, temperature, soot, and 
stability.  Conducting the tests in microgravity allows for great simplifications in the analysis of 
ion-driven convection and flame interaction, enabling new understanding and the development 
of less polluting and more efficient combustion technology for use on Earth.

metadata.source: 22 ACME E-FIELD Flames/Reports/E-FIELD Flames Final Report.pdf
metadata.relative_path: 22 ACME E-FIELD Flames/Reports/E-FIELD Flames Final Report.pdf

text:
ACME/E-FIELD Flames Final Report (2019) 
 
10 April 2021 
44 
 
 
An electric field can strongly influence flames because of its effect on the ions produced as a 
result of the combustion reactions. The induced ion wind can modify the flame shape, alter the 
soot and stability limits, and direct the heat transfer.  The purpose of the E-FIELD Flames 
experiment is to gain an improved understanding of flame ion production and learn how the 
electric field can be used to manipulate the ions and control non-premixed flames for practical 
benefit.  For example, electric fields can enable stable burner operation at fuel-lean conditions 
with reduced pollutant emission, i.e., where the flame is not reliably sustained without the 
electric field.  As another example, the role of electric fields on soot formation can be dramatic.  
It appears that the ion driven wind alters the local convection and strongly influences the 
residence time of the soot precursors within the hot flame.  The experiment contributes to our 
critical understanding of combustion processes in the presence of electric fields. 
 
More specifically, E-FIELD Flames has the following experimental objectives: 
A. Determine the relationship between electric field voltage and chemi-ion current as 
functions of total fuel (methane and ethylene) flow rate and the amount of inert 
(nitrogen) in the fuel. 
B. Obtain the time response of the flame chemiluminescence, luminosity, and the ion 
current to large step changes in voltage, as functions of total fuel (methane and ethylene) 
flow rate and amount of inert (nitrogen) added to the fuel stream. 
C. Evaluate and manipulate sooting behavior (i.e., soot volume fraction and location of

metadata.source: 22 ACME E-FIELD Flames/Reports/E-FIELD Flames Final Report.pdf
metadata.relative_path: 22 ACME E-FIELD Flames/Reports/E-FIELD Flames Final Report.pdf

text:
current to large step changes in voltage, as functions of total fuel (methane and ethylene) 
flow rate and amount of inert (nitrogen) added to the fuel stream. 
C. Evaluate and manipulate sooting behavior (i.e., soot volume fraction and location of 
luminous soot) in relation to the electric field voltage and chemi-ion current as functions 
of total fuel (methane and ethylene) flow rate and amount of inert (nitrogen) added to 
the fuel stream. 
D. Use the variation of the chemi-ion current as a function of applied voltage to characterize 
the combustion behavior of near-limit lifted flames and use the associated ion-driven 
wind to stabilize or reattach these flames. 
 
The effect of the electric field on the flame is studied through tests conducted with a range of 
flame and electric field conditions.  The fuel, fuel jet velocity, air flow, electric-field voltage and 
polarity are the primary parameters of the E-FIELD Flames experiment.  Tests are conducted with 
methane and ethylene, including nitrogen dilutions of each, which provide a broad range of soot-
producing conditions, i.e., from soot-free to highly sooting.  They are conducted with both a 
simple gas-jet burner and the coflow burner that was also used for the Coflow Laminar Diffusion 
Flame (CLD Flame) experiment.  Tests with the coflow burner is conducted with and without a 
coflow of air, where the results of the latter are compared with those from the gas-jet burner to 
assess the effect of air entrainment on the flame.  The coflow burner also provides a different 
electrode configuration (close to a plane-to-plane) than the jet burner (close to a point-to-plane).  
In a typical test, the mesh electrode is energized at increasing potentials (relative to the burner),

metadata.source: 22 ACME E-FIELD Flames/Reports/E-FIELD Flames Final Report.pdf
metadata.relative_path: 22 ACME E-FIELD Flames/Reports/E-FIELD Flames Final Report.pdf

text:
electrode configuration (close to a plane-to-plane) than the jet burner (close to a point-to-plane).  
In a typical test, the mesh electrode is energized at increasing potentials (relative to the burner), 
where the flame’s response (e.g., ion current, luminosity, shape) to the resulting field strength is 
measured.  The field strength is changed in repeated steps or is instead smoothly ramped. 
 
Microgravity studies of flames allow for a range of simplifications and provide various advantages 
over normal-gravity studies.  For example, the flicker of flames, which is a buoyancy-driven (i.e.,

metadata.source: 22 ACME E-FIELD Flames/Reports/E-FIELD Flames Final Report.pdf
metadata.relative_path: 22 ACME E-FIELD Flames/Reports/E-FIELD Flames Final Report.pdf

text:
ACME/E-FIELD Flames Final Report (2019) 
 
10 April 2021 
45 
 
gravity-driven) instability, is eliminated yielding quasi-steady flames in microgravity.  
Microgravity flame flicker is then the result of electric body forces alone.  Length scales are 
increased in microgravity flames facilitating analysis of the flame structure.  Momentum-
dominated flames, which are important for most practical combustion, can be studied at low 
velocities to simplify analysis.  Microgravity flames tend to have a much stronger sensitivity to 
their atmosphere and exhibit a much broader range of characteristics than normal-gravity flames 
because of the near absence of buoyant entrainment.  The long residence times in microgravity 
flames can lead to strong soot production, but many microgravity flames are soot free.  The 
absence of buoyancy makes microgravity flames advantageous for studies of limit and stability 
behavior where chemical kinetics are important.  With these advantages, microgravity testing 
can lead to new understanding of the complex nature of combustion – regardless of the 
gravitational environment of the combustion application.  Chemi-ion species, electronically 
excited chemiluminescent species are very low concentration in typical flames, making the 
reduced buoyancy environment valuable for evaluating the minor species chemistry. 
 
 
II.  Methods/Research Operations 
  
A. Discussion of Method/Protocol 
E-FIELD Flames and other ACME experiments are configured, but not conducted, by the 
ISS crew.  The crew’s role is to set up the hardware, gas bottles, etc. for each set of tests.  
The most common changes include the gas bottles on the Combustion Integrated Rack 
(CIR) and the mass flow controllers on the modular ACME chamber insert.

metadata.source: 22 ACME E-FIELD Flames/Reports/E-FIELD Flames Final Report.pdf
metadata.relative_path: 22 ACME E-FIELD Flames/Reports/E-FIELD Flames Final Report.pdf

text:
The most common changes include the gas bottles on the Combustion Integrated Rack 
(CIR) and the mass flow controllers on the modular ACME chamber insert. 
 
All testing is commanded from the ground, specifically from the Glenn ISS Payload 
Operations Center (GIPOC).  The science portion of the testing is typically conducted in a 
nominally automated mode using pre-programmed scripts.  However, it may alternately 
be conducted in a ‘manual’ mode, where changes are made to a control parameter in 
response to the analog video downlink and the numerical data available in the telemetry 
stream.  For example, the mesh voltage can be adjusted to approach a flame’s stability or 
soot limit.  This was not done during Increments 55-56, where the console commanding 
during a test was typically limited to halting the test when it was observed in the analog 
ops video that the flame had extinguished. 
 
Testing is not conducted when thrusters fire or spacecraft dock or undock from ISS to 
ensure an acceptable acceleration environment. 
 
Data is downlinked between each set of tests, i.e., day of testing, to allow for preliminary 
analysis and requisite planning for subsequent testing.

ACME/E-FIELD Flames Final Report (2019) 
 
10 April 2021 
46 
 
III.  Results 
A. Baselined Activities Completed – Pre-flight, In-flight, Post-Flight 
A total of 142 flames were ignited for the E-FIELD Flames experiment during Increments 
55 and 56.  The first round of testing occurred from March to May 2018, which was 
followed by a second round, which began in September 2018 and was still underway at 
the beginning of Increment 57.  The first round of tests resulted in 120 ignited flames 
conducted with the same coflow burner used by the Coflow Laminar Diffusion Flame (CLD 
Flame) experiment, where CLD Flame’s second round occurred between the two rounds 
of the E-FIELD Flames experiment.  The ‘interruption’ in the E-FIELD Flames testing was 
intentionally planned years in advance to enable the PI team to review the initial results 
in detail and with that knowledge plan the second round of tests to maximize its scientific 
outcome. 
 
E-FIELD Flames does not have living subjects like a life science experiment, but the tests 
are independently conducted with two different gaseous fuels, methane and ethylene.  
Both are simple hydrocarbon gases for which the chemistry is well understood.  Methane 
(CH4) is the primary component of natural gas and tends to produce low levels of soot 
given the absence of carbon-carbon bonds.  Meanwhile, ethylene (C2H4), is highly sooting 
because of its carbon double bond.  For both fuels, tests were conducted with pure fuel 
and fuel mixed with nitrogen over a broad range of dilutions.  For limited cases, the fuel 
and nitrogen was premixed on the ground prior to launch.  ACME bottles were launched 
with methane concentrations of 30%, 40%, 45%, and 100% with a balance of nitrogen (on

metadata.source: 22 ACME E-FIELD Flames/Reports/E-FIELD Flames Final Report.pdf
metadata.relative_path: 22 ACME E-FIELD Flames/Reports/E-FIELD Flames Final Report.pdf

text:
and nitrogen was premixed on the ground prior to launch.  ACME bottles were launched 
with methane concentrations of 30%, 40%, 45%, and 100% with a balance of nitrogen (on 
a volume basis).  Similarly, bottles were launched with ethylene concentrations of 30%, 
50%, and 100%, again with a balance of nitrogen (on a volume basis).  But the ACME 
hardware also allows for simultaneous flow of fuel and nitrogen to the burner, allowing 
for on-orbit fuel dilution and testing at a continuum of fuel concentrations.  In all cases, 
the coflow was 21% oxygen with a balance of nitrogen (on a volume basis).  
 
There are no samples (e.g., of soot) collected for E-FIELD Flames, where all of the ISS 
results are electronically transmitted to the ground.  That is furthermore the case for all 
currently planned ACME experiments. 
 
A summary log of the E-FIELD Flames ignited for E-FIELD Flames during Increments 55 and 
56, including a limited overview of the test conditions, is found on the next page in Table 
1.

1. Mission anomalies  
The primary hard drive for the CIR’s IPSU-G Image Processing and Storage Unit - for 
Gigabit Ethernet (GigE) cameras – failed to boot on April 27, 2018 (18117).  For ACME 
experiments, the IPSU-G is used for two key cameras, the ACME color digital ‘data’

Gigabit Ethernet (GigE) cameras – failed to boot on April 27, 2018 (18117).  For ACME

which is used for CLD Flame with a narrow bandpass filter to image CH*

May 7 (18127) by the removal of that primary drive.  The removed drive was 
reinstalled on Aug. 14 (18226) by astronaut Ricky Arnold during the second round of 
CLD Flame testing.  Although the hard drive was installed in the secondary position,

text:
ACME/E-FIELD Flames Final Report (2019) 
 
10 April 2021 
48 
 
The CIR’s IPSU-1 Image Processing and Storage Unit, which is used with the High Bit-
Depth Multispectral (HiBMs) camera and the collimated illumination package, was 
only intermittently operable in mid-Sept. 2018 and was not operable at the start of E-
FIELD Flames’ second round.  Those capabilities were not seen as critical for E-FIELD 
Flames, where the illumination is significantly blocked by the mounting bracket for 
the mesh electrode.  Therefore, the tests on Sept. 26 (18269) and Oct. 1 (18274) were 
conducted without HiBMs imaging or the CIR illumination.  It was later determined to 
be an issue with a cable connection, which was corrected by astronaut Alex Gerst on 
Oct. 22 (18295) when he carried out other ACME tasks. 
 
2. Any other difficulties in obtaining scientific data   
E-FIELD Flames tests sometimes automatically abort (due to the controlling software 
script), where that is typically prior to gas flow and the activation of the igniter.  As a 
result, there is little lost other than the time in the failed test attempt.   The aborts 
normally occur because of communication issues with IPSU-1.  These are infrequent, 
but there are some days when tests abort repeatedly.  
 
Tests are of course also unsuccessful when the flame fails to ignite.  The first test of 
the day has sometimes failed to ignite, presumably because the fuel line has not been 
sufficiently primed.  Ignition is sometimes unsuccessful because the settings for the 
automatic flame detection are such that detection threshold is reached because of 
the igniter glow rather than a flame.  As a result of the detection, the hot-wire igniter

metadata.source: 22 ACME E-FIELD Flames/Reports/E-FIELD Flames Final Report.pdf
metadata.relative_path: 22 ACME E-FIELD Flames/Reports/E-FIELD Flames Final Report.pdf

text:
automatic flame detection are such that detection threshold is reached because of 
the igniter glow rather than a flame.  As a result of the detection, the hot-wire igniter 
is deactivated and retracted, which is of course an issue if the flame has yet to ignite.  
This is typically avoided by detecting ignition with measurement of the flame’s OH* 
chemiluminescence with a Photomultiplier Tube (PMT) module.  The OH* 
chemiluminescence, in the ultraviolet at 310 nm, is a good indicator of an ignited 
flame rather than the glowing igniter, which emits primarily in the infrared and visible 
spectrum.  However, the combination of igniter settings and PMT gains can lead to 
false ignition detection. 
 
ACME’s Mass Flow Controllers (MFCs) used to control the flow of fuel, nitrogen, and 
synthetic air (i.e., 21% oxygen with a balance of nitrogen, on a volume basis) have 
unfortunately not always performed adequately.  The fuel and especially nitrogen 
flows sometimes oscillate. Furthermore, the MFC used for the ‘air’ coflow behaves as 
if it is sticking in a few places, where the flow rate won’t linearly ramp when 
commanded (as required for the CLD Flame experiment).  It tends to stick in some 
places and then abruptly overshoot where that has sometimes been seen to 
extinguish the flame.  As a result, mass flow controllers are tested - without flames - 
after they are first installed.  Adjustments are often then made to (1) the settings that 
control when the valves open and (2) the Proportional-Integral-Derivative (PID) 
settings.  This activity has involved significant testing, separate from flame tests, and 
has taken place during CLD Flame operations on 17333, 17334, 17347, 17354, 18008,

metadata.source: 22 ACME E-FIELD Flames/Reports/E-FIELD Flames Final Report.pdf
metadata.relative_path: 22 ACME E-FIELD Flames/Reports/E-FIELD Flames Final Report.pdf

text:
settings.  This activity has involved significant testing, separate from flame tests, and 
has taken place during CLD Flame operations on 17333, 17334, 17347, 17354, 18008, 
18022, 18038, 18046, 18143, and 18241.  In this regard, there are an assortment of 
MFCs with different flow ranges for each of the three gases.  While the MFC tuning

metadata.source: 22 ACME E-FIELD Flames/Reports/E-FIELD Flames Final Report.pdf
metadata.relative_path: 22 ACME E-FIELD Flames/Reports/E-FIELD Flames Final Report.pdf

text:
ACME/E-FIELD Flames Final Report (2019) 
 
10 April 2021 
49 
 
has been beneficial in some cases, it has not eliminated all gas flow problems.  It was 
seen that nitrogen oscillations tend to damp with time, so a nitrogen pre-flow was 
implemented so that the oscillations would typically end before the flame 
measurements.  That approach has been partially successful and was introduced 
during E-FIELD Flames’ first round.  Later, a procedure of re-zeroing the MFCs prior to 
each test was also implemented during E-FIELD Flames’ second round.  A replacement 
MFC for the ‘air’ coflow is being prepared for spaceflight, where a limited third round 
of CLD Flame testing is being planned to accomplish its extinction limit objective.  
 
The final day of testing during E-FIELD Flame’s first round was conducted with highly 
sooty ethylene flames and a positively charged mesh, which tends to push the flame 
down toward the burner.  A significant amount of soot deposited on the burner, both 
on the inner tube from which the fuel issues as well as the honeycomb in the burner 
annulus from which the air flows.  The extent of the soot wasn’t appreciated until 
flame testing for CLD Flame’s second round began on May 25 (18145).  Additional 
evaluation tests were performed on May 31 (18151), and the decision was made to 
have the crew clean the soot from the burner because it was clear that the gas flow 
from the burner was affected by the soot buildup.  A cleaning procedure was 
developed, approved, and carried out by astronaut Ricky Arnold on June 19 (18170).  
The cleaned burner was imaged with the CIR cameras on June 21 (18172), but the 
evaluation testing was deferred because of a cable mating issue.  The cable mating

metadata.source: 22 ACME E-FIELD Flames/Reports/E-FIELD Flames Final Report.pdf
metadata.relative_path: 22 ACME E-FIELD Flames/Reports/E-FIELD Flames Final Report.pdf

text:
developed, approved, and carried out by astronaut Ricky Arnold on June 19 (18170).  
The cleaned burner was imaged with the CIR cameras on June 21 (18172), but the 
evaluation testing was deferred because of a cable mating issue.  The cable mating 
was corrected by Arnold on June 25 (18176) and the evaluation testing of the cleaned 
burner was conducted on the following day, June 26 (18177).  Regular flame testing 
in CLD Flame’s second round finally commenced on July 5 (18186), six weeks after the 
soot accumulation was identified as an issue.  However, useful scientific results were 
obtained on the June 26 evaluation day, so the burner cleaning effectively led to a 1- 
month delay. 
 
C. Completeness/Quality of Data 
The number of flames ignited significantly exceeds the planned tests which were (1) 
specified as required in the ACME Integrated Science Requirements Document (ISRD), 
using the gas-jet burner, and (2) later expanded to include tests with the coflow burner 
to partially make up for science loss resulting from the slow response time of the high-
voltage power supply.  Following the revision, a total of 74 E-FIELD Flames tests were 
identified as required.  In contrast, 120 flames were ignited in the experiment’s first 
round, i.e., first half.  In that round, roughly 200% more flames were ignited than had 
been planned.  
 
It should be understood that a complete set of image data is not available for all tests.  As 
discussed in section III.B, the IPSU-1 was not working at the beginning of the second round 
of testing, preventing use of both the HiBMs camera and the CIR’s collimated illumination 
package.  Those are not critical for E-FIELD Flames, so tests continued without their use.

text:
ACME/E-FIELD Flames Final Report (2019) 
 
10 April 2021 
50 
 
Furthermore, recorded image data is sometimes deleted without downlinking.  This is 
done because of operational constraints which limit the amount of data that can be 
managed per test day.  Given the constraint, the decision is sometimes made to sacrifice 
some image data (e.g., from the HiBMs camera) to allow additional tests to be conducted.  
This is intentionally done in order to maximize the scientific return of each day of testing 
within the project constraints. 
 
Data quality is of course dependent on the experimental hardware.  But neglecting that 
limitation on data quality, the cameras are sensitive to radiation where pixels gradually 
become ‘hot’ over time.  While these bright spots are addressed in image post-processing, 
they are a degradation of the image quality. 
 
It is possible that the tests are subtly affected by the acceleration environment, but there 
is not obvious indication of this and it has thus far not been evaluated with available 
measurements from the Space Acceleration Measurement System (SAMS).  In this regard, 
note that the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR), in which the experiment is conducted, is 
equipped with a Passive Rack Isolation System (PaRIS).  
 
Regardless of the shortcomings discussed above, a great wealth of experimental data has 
been secured and E-FIELD Flames is considered to be highly successful. 
 
D. Status of Data Analysis 
Data from the E-FIELD Flames experiments includes video recordings from the operations 
camera for general flame behavior, the ACME data camera for high resolution images at 
various exposures and frame rates as dictated by the flame luminosity, intensified camera

metadata.source: 22 ACME E-FIELD Flames/Reports/E-FIELD Flames Final Report.pdf
metadata.relative_path: 22 ACME E-FIELD Flames/Reports/E-FIELD Flames Final Report.pdf

text:
camera for general flame behavior, the ACME data camera for high resolution images at 
various exposures and frame rates as dictated by the flame luminosity, intensified camera 
images and non-imaging data at 100 Hz.  The non-imaging data is extracted using Matlab 
scripts (modified from those developed by CLD Flame researchers) to show trends of ion 
current and flame luminosity as a function of the applied field, and the flame parameters 
(fuel, flowrate, burner type).  Image data is processed using the OMA software (also 
developed and used by CLD Flame researchers).   
 
The overall data volume is large with a storage limit of 127,000 MB per test day, the data 
has been downloaded to the hard drive with a backup system at UC Irvine.  At this stage, 
with operations ongoing, the analysis is comparative and qualitative, just to show the 
major differences in behavior in microgravity and normal-gravity (1-g) flames. 
 
E. Preliminary Research Findings 
Results from the early E-FIELD Flame experiments have demonstrated clear differences 
between normal-gravity and microgravity flame behaviors.  A few examples include the 
distinct maximum of ion current for co-flow burner flames in microgravity, where the 1-g 
flames more smoothly reach a saturation condition.  The results also show that the 
electric body force can produce flame oscillations similar to those driven by buoyancy in 
normal gravity, and microgravity flame shapes with an electric field can mimic normal-

10 April 2021 
51 
 
gravity flames without electric fields.  Burner type plays a role in the flame/field 
interaction, and in particular, reversing the field polarity for the jet flame does not 
produce an inverted result over the entire voltage range tested.  Results also demonstrate 
the interactions between electric fields and soot are more complex in microgravity.  At 
the same time, the preliminary findings suggest that some of the key expectations 
generally hold (e.g., ion current scales approximately with flow rate for a fixed fuel and 
burner).

This section only includes representative findings as the ISS experiments covered a wide 
range of conditions and outcomes.  Color camera images, intensified camera images, total

were recorded in all cases.  Figure 1 gives example flame images from the first tests 
conducted with methane as fuel.  Two fuel flow rates are shown, with the voltage 
indicated as nominal field strength (kV/cm).  Since the physical spacing from the burner 
to the mesh is 37 mm, 2 kV/cm represents 7000 V across the flame.

The key measurement for the E-FIELD Flames experiments is the ion current as a function 
of applied voltage, i.e., the voltage-current or V-I curve.  This curve provides information 
on the flames ability to produce chemi-ions based on its saturation ion current, and it 
provides a measure of combustion performance in that ion production is a function of 
carbon influx into the flame and the vigorousness of the combustion process.  More 
compact, higher temperature flames produce more chemi-ions than do larger more 
diffuse reaction zones of lower overall temperature for the same fuel flow.  The first effect 
(i.e., the relationship between carbon influx and peak ion current) can be seen in Figure 
2, where the flow of 15 cm/s methane produces slightly above 2 microamps of ion current 
at the peak (1.5 kV/cm) and the flow of 19 cm/s methane has a peak of 2.75 microamps.  
While the ratio is not exact, the peak ion current is nearly proportional to the flow

metadata.source: 22 ACME E-FIELD Flames/Reports/E-FIELD Flames Final Report.pdf

10 April 2021 
52 
 
velocity.  Another interesting feature of these curves is the peak value.  Traditional 
electrical aspects of flames studies look for a saturation ion current plateau, where the 
ion current remains fixed despite an increase in applied electric field.  For these 
microgravity flames, there is a pronounced peak in the ion current at saturation and then 
a gradual decrease to a global saturation plateau.  This is a strikingly different behavior 
than is seen in 1-g, and the behavior is even more pronounced for the case where there 
is zero coflow. 
 
 
Figure 2. Ion current as a function of the field strength and fuel velocity with a 3.1 cm/s 
coflow. (a) 15 cm/s methane. (b) 19 cm/s methane. 
 
As can be seen in Figure 3, which is the same V-I curve result in microgravity for the case 
where there is no coflowing air, and Figure 4 shows the flame images.  These figures again 
show a reasonably linear scaling of peak ion current with fuel flow velocity, but they 
demonstrate a very pronounced peak ion current with a rapid drop to a global saturation 
ion current plateau.  Since these are diffusion flames, essentially all of the fuel is being 
burned independent of the flame’s shape and the applied electric field, but it seems clear 
that the electric field is affecting the chemi-ion production capability of the flame.  As is 
apparent from the flame images, the flame is most compact at the voltage consistent with 
the peak ion current.  With increasing voltage, the flame becomes less compact and the 
ion current decreases.  We presume that the flame remains at saturation throughout this 
period (that is, the flame is producing as many ions as it can, and those ions are being

metadata.relative_path: 22 ACME E-FIELD Flames/Reports/E-FIELD Flames Final Report.pdf

text:
ion current decreases.  We presume that the flame remains at saturation throughout this 
period (that is, the flame is producing as many ions as it can, and those ions are being 
removed from the reaction zone as soon as they are created) so the decrease in ion 
current results from a change in combustion intensity.  We can explore this hypothesis 
further using the PMT data collected in the experiments.

(1) The ion current reaches a peak at approximately the same field strength for both 
velocities in 1-g while in microgravity the ion current peak for a lower fuel velocity 
occurs at a lower field strength.  The field strength at the peak current seems to scale 
linearly with the fuel velocity. 
 
 
Figure 5. Ion current as a function of field strength and fuel velocity with no coflow in 
normal gravity. (a) 16 cm/s methane. (b) 19 cm/s methane. 
 
(2) In microgravity, the ion current does not smoothly increase to saturation nor does it 
show a gentle peak with a mild decrease as is seen in the normal gravity results.  
Instead, in microgravity there is a distinct peak in the ion current with a severe 
decrease throughout the saturation condition, with a final saturation plateau 
observed at voltages substantially above the voltage at peak ion current.  That is, the 
microgravity final saturation is not the maximum ion current observed.  This 
difference is more dramatic when there is no coflow, which suggests that entrainment 
plays an important role whether caused by buoyancy or a forced coflow.  
 
(3) The peak ion current is higher for microgravity than comparison 1-g flames.  The 
reason is not obvious at this point but may result from a more focused upward flow 
from the electric body force and ion-driven wind as compared to the combined effects 
of the ion wind and buoyancy. 
 
(4) The peak ion current is approximately proportional to fuel flow velocity, which, as 
described in prior studies, reflects the relationship between ion production and the 
carbon flux into the system.  The peak ion current also increases with the coflow which

metadata.relative_path: 22 ACME E-FIELD Flames/Reports/E-FIELD Flames Final Report.pdf

text:
described in prior studies, reflects the relationship between ion production and the 
carbon flux into the system.  The peak ion current also increases with the coflow which 
suggests that healthier oxidizer transport helps increase the ion production.

The results from ethylene flames with coflow are shown in Figures 6 and 7, positive field 
and negative field respectively.  At 15 cm/s, the ion current reaches a peak around 2.7 
microamps which is similar to the 19 cm/s 100% methane coflow air case but with only 
0.4 of the volumetric carbon content.  The results for 15 cm/s also presents a rapid 
parabolic behavior after reaching the saturation peak.  In the negative field case, the peak 
ion current decreases to 0.56 of the positive field case at the same flow rate 19 cm/s (or 
0.4 for 15 cm/s).  Another aspect is that the ion current peaks sooner for the higher flow 
rate/carbon content in the negative field configuration as compared to the positive field 
experiments.  These phenomena, particularly for the positive field strength have not yet 
been measured in the laboratory at 1-g.  The difference in behavior appears to be related 
to the removal of the buoyancy force so that the momentum flow coupled with the ion 
driven flow tends to resettle under the electric field body force. Detailed analysis is 
underway.

Electric-Field Effects on Laminar Diffusion Flames 
E-FIELD Flames is one of several independent experiments that are part of the ACME project, 
which uses a single modular set of hardware to carry out studies of flames burning gaseous fuels 
in the ISS’ Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR).  The investigation was carried out in two rounds of 
tests, where the first (with ACME’s coflow burner) occurred in Increment 55 and the second (with 
a gas-jet burner) began in Increment 56 and ended in Increment 57.  As a result, there is nothing 
to be reported for Increment 58.

Scientist, who is the primary contact for E-FIELD Flames and ACME information.

I.  Introduction 
The Electric-Field Effects on Laminar Diffusion Flames (E-FIELD Flames) experiment was 
conducted in the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) on the International Space Station, as part of

text:
I.  Introduction 
The Electric-Field Effects on Laminar Diffusion Flames (E-FIELD Flames) experiment was 
conducted in the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) on the International Space Station, as part of 
the Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) project.  In this experiment, an 
electric field with voltages as high as 10,000 volts was established between the burner and a flat, 
circular mesh electrode suspended above (i.e., downstream of) the burner.  The motion of the 
charged ions, which are naturally produced within the flame, are strongly affected by a strong 
electric field.  The resulting ion-driven wind can dramatically influence the stability and sooting 
behavior of the flame.  Measurements were made of electric-field strength, the ion current 
passing through the flame, and flame characteristics such as the size, structure, temperature, 
soot, and stability.  Conducting the tests in microgravity allowed for great simplifications in the

metadata.source: 22 ACME E-FIELD Flames/Reports/E-FIELD Flames Final Report.pdf
metadata.relative_path: 22 ACME E-FIELD Flames/Reports/E-FIELD Flames Final Report.pdf

text:
ACME/E-FIELD Flames Final Report (2019) 
 
10 April 2021 
59 
 
analysis of ion-driven convection and flame interaction, enabling new understanding and the 
development of less polluting and more efficient combustion technology for use on Earth. 
 
An electric field can strongly influence flames because of its effect on the ions produced as a 
result of the combustion reactions. The induced ion wind can modify the flame shape, alter the 
soot and stability limits, and direct the heat transfer.  The purpose of the E-FIELD Flames 
experiment is to gain an improved understanding of flame ion production and learn how the 
electric field can be used to manipulate the ions and control non-premixed flames for practical 
benefit.  For example, electric fields can enable stable burner operation at fuel-lean conditions 
with reduced pollutant emission, i.e., where the flame is not reliably sustained without the 
electric field.  As another example, the role of electric fields on soot formation can be dramatic.  
It appears that the ion driven wind alters the local convection and strongly influences the 
residence time of the soot precursors within the hot flame.  The experiment contributes to our 
critical understanding of combustion processes in the presence of electric fields. 
 
More specifically, E-FIELD Flames has the following experimental objectives: 
A. Determine the relationship between electric field voltage and chemi-ion current as 
functions of total fuel (methane and ethylene) flow rate and the amount of inert 
(nitrogen) in the fuel. 
B. Obtain the time response of the flame chemiluminescence, luminosity, and the ion 
current to large step changes in voltage, as functions of total fuel (methane and ethylene)

metadata.source: 22 ACME E-FIELD Flames/Reports/E-FIELD Flames Final Report.pdf
metadata.relative_path: 22 ACME E-FIELD Flames/Reports/E-FIELD Flames Final Report.pdf

text:
(nitrogen) in the fuel. 
B. Obtain the time response of the flame chemiluminescence, luminosity, and the ion 
current to large step changes in voltage, as functions of total fuel (methane and ethylene) 
flow rate and amount of inert (nitrogen) added to the fuel stream. 
C. Evaluate and manipulate sooting behavior (i.e., soot volume fraction and location of 
luminous soot) in relation to the electric field voltage and chemi-ion current as functions 
of total fuel (methane and ethylene) flow rate and amount of inert (nitrogen) added to 
the fuel stream. 
D. Use the variation of the chemi-ion current as a function of applied voltage to characterize 
the combustion behavior of near-limit lifted flames and use the associated ion-driven 
wind to stabilize or reattach these flames. 
 
The effect of the electric field on the flame is studied through tests conducted with a range of 
flame and electric field conditions.  The fuel, fuel jet velocity, air flow, electric-field voltage and 
polarity were the primary parameters of the E-FIELD Flames experiment.  Tests were conducted 
with methane and ethylene, including nitrogen dilutions of each, which provide a broad range of 
soot-producing conditions, i.e., from soot-free to highly sooting.  They were carried out with both 
a simple gas-jet burner and the coflow burner that was also used for the Coflow Laminar Diffusion 
Flame (CLD Flame) experiment.  Tests with the coflow burner were conducted with and without 
a coflow of air, where the results of the latter are compared with those from the gas-jet burner 
to assess the effect of air entrainment on the flame.  The coflow burner also provided a different 
electrode configuration (close to a plane-to-plane) than the jet burner (close to a point-to-plane).

metadata.source: 22 ACME E-FIELD Flames/Reports/E-FIELD Flames Final Report.pdf
metadata.relative_path: 22 ACME E-FIELD Flames/Reports/E-FIELD Flames Final Report.pdf

text:
to assess the effect of air entrainment on the flame.  The coflow burner also provided a different 
electrode configuration (close to a plane-to-plane) than the jet burner (close to a point-to-plane).  
In a typical test, the mesh electrode was energized at increasing potentials (relative to the 
burner), where the flame’s response (e.g., ion current, luminosity, shape) to the resulting field 
strength was measured.  The field strength was changed in repeated steps or was instead 
smoothly ramped.

text:
ACME/E-FIELD Flames Final Report (2019) 
 
10 April 2021 
60 
 
 
Microgravity studies of flames allow for a range of simplifications and provide various advantages 
over normal-gravity studies.  For example, the natural flicker of flames, which is a buoyancy-
driven (i.e., gravity-driven) instability, is eliminated yielding quasi-steady flames in microgravity.  
Therefore, the flicker in the E-FIELD Flames was a result of electric body forces alone.  Length 
scales are increased in microgravity flames facilitating analysis of the flame structure.  
Momentum-dominated flames, which are important for most practical combustion, can be 
studied at low velocities to simplify analysis.  Microgravity flames tend to have a much stronger 
sensitivity to their atmosphere and exhibit a much broader range of characteristics than normal-
gravity flames because of the near absence of buoyant entrainment.  The long residence times in 
microgravity flames can lead to strong soot production, but many microgravity flames are soot 
free.  The absence of buoyancy makes microgravity flames advantageous for studies of limit and 
stability behavior where chemical kinetics are important.  For example, chemi-ion species, 
electronically excited chemiluminescent species, are at very low concentration in typical flames, 
making the reduced buoyancy environment valuable for evaluating the minor species chemistry.  
With these advantages, microgravity testing can lead to new understanding of the complex 
nature of combustion – regardless of the gravitational environment of the combustion 
application. 
 
 
II.  Methods/Research Operations 
  
A. Discussion of Method/Protocol 
E-FIELD Flames and other ACME experiments are configured, but not conducted, by the

metadata.source: 22 ACME E-FIELD Flames/Reports/E-FIELD Flames Final Report.pdf
metadata.relative_path: 22 ACME E-FIELD Flames/Reports/E-FIELD Flames Final Report.pdf

text:
application. 
 
 
II.  Methods/Research Operations 
  
A. Discussion of Method/Protocol 
E-FIELD Flames and other ACME experiments are configured, but not conducted, by the 
ISS crew.  The crew’s role is to set up the hardware, gas bottles, etc. for each set of tests.  
The most common changes include the gas bottles on the Combustion Integrated Rack 
(CIR) and the mass flow controllers on the modular ACME chamber insert. 
 
All testing is commanded from the ground, specifically from the Glenn ISS Payload 
Operations Center (GIPOC).  The science portion of the testing is typically conducted in a 
nominally automated mode using pre-programmed scripts.  However, it may alternately 
be conducted in a ‘manual’ mode, where changes are made to a control parameter in 
response to the analog video downlink and the numerical data available in the telemetry 
stream.  For example, the mesh voltage can be adjusted to approach a flame’s stability or 
soot limit.  This was not done during Increments 55-56 or 57-58, where the console 
commanding during a test was typically limited to halting the test when it was observed 
in the analog ops video that the flame had extinguished. 
 
Testing is not conducted when thrusters fire or spacecraft dock or undock from ISS to 
ensure an acceptable acceleration environment. 
 
Data is downlinked between each set of tests, i.e., day of testing, to allow for preliminary 
analysis and requisite planning for subsequent testing.

text:
ACME/E-FIELD Flames Final Report (2019) 
 
10 April 2021 
61 
 
  
III.  Results 
A. Baselined Activities Completed – Pre-flight, In-flight, Post-Flight 
A total of 219 flames were ignited for the E-FIELD Flames experiment, with 142 and 77 
respectively ignited during Increments 55-56 and 57-58.  Note that the investigation’s 
testing was completed during Increment 57, so no flames were ignited during Increment 
58.  The first and second rounds of testing respectively occurred in March-May 2018 and 
September-November 2018.  The two rounds of tests resulted in 120 and 99 ignited 
flames conducted with coflow and gas-jet burners, respectively.  The coflow burner was 
developed for the Coflow Laminar Diffusion Flame (CLD Flame) experiment, where CLD 
Flames’ second round occurred between the two rounds of the E-FIELD Flames 
experiment.  The ‘interruption’ in the E-FIELD Flames testing was intentionally planned 
years in advance to enable the PI team to review the initial results in detail and with that 
knowledge plan the second round of tests to maximize its scientific outcome. 
 
E-FIELD Flames does not have living subjects like a life science experiment, but the tests 
are independently conducted with two different gaseous fuels, methane and ethylene.  
Both are simple hydrocarbon gases for which the chemistry is well understood.  Methane 
(CH4) is the primary component of natural gas and tends to produce low levels of soot 
given the absence of carbon-carbon bonds.  Meanwhile, ethylene (C2H4), is highly sooting 
because of its carbon double bond.  For both fuels, tests were conducted with pure fuel 
and fuel mixed with nitrogen over a broad range of dilutions.  For limited cases, the fuel

metadata.source: 22 ACME E-FIELD Flames/Reports/E-FIELD Flames Final Report.pdf
metadata.relative_path: 22 ACME E-FIELD Flames/Reports/E-FIELD Flames Final Report.pdf

text:
because of its carbon double bond.  For both fuels, tests were conducted with pure fuel 
and fuel mixed with nitrogen over a broad range of dilutions.  For limited cases, the fuel 
and nitrogen was premixed on the ground prior to launch.  ACME bottles were launched 
with methane concentrations of 30%, 40%, 45%, and 100% with a balance of nitrogen (on 
a volume basis).  Similarly, bottles were launched with ethylene concentrations of 30%, 
50%, and 100%, again with a balance of nitrogen (on a volume basis).  But the ACME 
hardware also allows for simultaneous flow of fuel and nitrogen to the burner, allowing 
for on-orbit fuel dilution and testing at a continuum of fuel concentrations.  In all cases, 
the coflow was 21% oxygen with a balance of nitrogen (on a volume basis).  
 
No samples (e.g., of soot) were collected for E-FIELD Flames; all of the ISS results were 
electronically transmitted to the ground.  That is furthermore the case for all currently 
planned ACME experiments. 
 
A summary log of the E-FIELD Flames ignited for E-FIELD Flames during Increments 55-57, 
including a limited overview of the test conditions, is found on the next page in Table 1.

3. Mission anomalies  
The CIR’s IPSU-1 Image Processing and Storage Unit, which is used with the High Bit-
Depth Multispectral (HiBMs) camera and the collimated illumination package, was 
only intermittently operable at the end of Increment 56 and was not operable at the 
start of Increment 57.  Those capabilities were not seen as critical for E-FIELD Flames,

where the illumination is significantly blocked by the mounting bracket for the mesh 
electrode.  Therefore, the tests on Sept. 26 (18269), Oct. 1 (18274), Oct. 9 (18282), 
Oct. 12 (18285), and Oct. 17 (18290) were conducted without HiBMs imaging or the 
CIR illumination.  It was later determined to be an issue with a cable connection, which 
was corrected by astronaut Alex Gerst on Oct. 22 (18295) when he carried out other 
ACME tasks.  As a result, the subsequent E-FIELD Flames tests were carried out using 
the HiBMs camera and illumination package. 
 
4. Any other difficulties in obtaining scientific data   
E-FIELD Flames tests sometimes automatically aborted (due to the controlling 
software script), where that was typically prior to gas flow and the activation of the 
igniter.  As a result, there was little lost other than the time in the failed test attempt.   
The aborts normally occurred because of communication issues with IPSU-1.  These 
are infrequent, but there are some days when tests aborted repeatedly.  
 
Tests are of course also unsuccessful when the flame fails to ignite.  The first test of 
the day has sometimes failed to ignite, presumably because the fuel line has not been 
sufficiently primed.  Ignition was sometimes unsuccessful because the settings for the 
automatic flame detection are such that detection threshold is reached because of 
the igniter glow rather than a flame.  As a result of the detection, the hot-wire igniter 
is deactivated and retracted, which is of course an issue if the flame has yet to ignite.  
This is typically avoided by detecting ignition with measurement of the flame’s OH* 
chemiluminescence with a Photomultiplier Tube (PMT) module.  The OH*

metadata.source: 22 ACME E-FIELD Flames/Reports/E-FIELD Flames Final Report.pdf
metadata.relative_path: 22 ACME E-FIELD Flames/Reports/E-FIELD Flames Final Report.pdf

text:
is deactivated and retracted, which is of course an issue if the flame has yet to ignite.  
This is typically avoided by detecting ignition with measurement of the flame’s OH* 
chemiluminescence with a Photomultiplier Tube (PMT) module.  The OH* 
chemiluminescence, in the ultraviolet at 310 nm, is a good indicator of an ignited 
flame rather than the glowing igniter, which emits primarily in the infrared and visible 
spectrum.  However, the combination of igniter settings and PMT gains can lead to 
false ignition detection. 
 
ACME’s Mass Flow Controllers (MFCs) used to control the flow of fuel, nitrogen, and 
synthetic air (i.e., 21% oxygen with a balance of nitrogen, on a volume basis) have 
unfortunately not always performed adequately.  The fuel and especially nitrogen 
flows sometimes oscillate. Furthermore, the MFC used for the ‘air’ coflow behaves as 
if it is sticking in a few places, where the flow rate won’t linearly ramp when 
commanded (as required for the CLD Flame experiment).  It tends to stick in some 
places and then abruptly overshoot where that has sometimes been seen to 
extinguish the flame.  As a result, mass flow controllers are tested - without flames - 
after they are first installed.  Adjustments are often then made to (1) the settings that 
control when the valves open and (2) the Proportional-Integral-Derivative (PID) 
settings.  This ACME activity has involved significant testing, separate from flame 
tests, and has taken place on 17333, 17334, 17347, 17354, 18008, 18022, 18038, 
18046, 18143, 18241, 19059, and 19112.  In this regard, there are an assortment of 
MFCs with different flow ranges for each of the three gases.  While the MFC 
adjustments have been beneficial, they have not eliminated all gas flow problems.  It

MFCs with different flow ranges for each of the three gases.  While the MFC 
adjustments have been beneficial, they have not eliminated all gas flow problems.  It 
was seen that nitrogen oscillations tend to damp with time, so a nitrogen pre-flow

was implemented so that the oscillations would typically end before the flame 
measurements.  That approach was partially successful and was introduced during E-
FIELD Flames’ first round.  Later, a procedure of re-zeroing the MFCs prior to each test 
was also implemented during E-FIELD Flames’ second round.  A replacement MFC for 
the ‘air’ coflow is being prepared for spaceflight, where a limited third round of CLD 
Flame testing is being planned to accomplish its extinction limit objective.  
 
C. Completeness/Quality of Data 
The number of flames ignited significantly exceeds the planned tests which were (1) 
specified as required in the ACME Integrated Science Requirements Document (ISRD), 
using the gas-jet burner, and (2) later expanded to include tests with the coflow burner 
to partially make up for science loss resulting from the slow response time of the high-
voltage power supply.  Following the revision, a total of 74 E-FIELD Flames tests were 
identified as required.  In contrast, 219 flames were ignited in the experiment, so nearly 
three times as many flames were ignited than required.  
 
It should be understood that a complete set of image data is not available for all tests.  As 
discussed in section III.B, the IPSU-1 was not working at the beginning of the second round 
of testing, preventing use of both the HiBMs camera and the CIR’s collimated illumination 
package.  Those are not critical for E-FIELD Flames, so tests continued without their use. 
 
Furthermore, recorded image data is sometimes deleted without downlinking.  This is 
done because of operational constraints which limit the amount of data that can be

metadata.source: 22 ACME E-FIELD Flames/Reports/E-FIELD Flames Final Report.pdf
metadata.relative_path: 22 ACME E-FIELD Flames/Reports/E-FIELD Flames Final Report.pdf

text:
Furthermore, recorded image data is sometimes deleted without downlinking.  This is 
done because of operational constraints which limit the amount of data that can be 
managed per test day.  Given the constraint, the decision is sometimes made to sacrifice 
some image data (e.g., from the HiBMs camera) to allow additional tests to be conducted.  
This is intentionally done in order to maximize the scientific return of each day of testing 
within the project constraints. 
 
Data quality is of course dependent on the experimental hardware.  But neglecting that 
limitation on data quality, the cameras are sensitive to radiation where pixels gradually 
become ‘hot’ over time.  While these bright spots are addressed in image post-processing, 
they are a degradation of the image quality. 
 
It is possible that the tests are subtly affected by the acceleration environment, but there 
is not obvious indication of this and it has thus far not been evaluated with available 
measurements from the Space Acceleration Measurement System (SAMS).  In this regard, 
note that the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR), in which the experiment is conducted, is 
equipped with a Passive Rack Isolation System (PaRIS).  
 
Regardless of the shortcomings discussed above, a great wealth of experimental data has 
been secured and E-FIELD Flames is considered to be highly successful.

10 April 2021

D. Status of Data Analysis 
Data from the tests making up the E-FIELD Flames experiment includes video recordings 
from the operations camera for general flame behavior, high resolution images from the 
ACME data camera at various exposures and frame rates as dictated by the flame 
luminosity, intensified camera images, and non-imaging data at 125 Hz.  The non-imaging 
data file is processed using Matlab scripts (modified from those developed by CLD Flame 
researchers) to separately show trends of ion current and flame luminosity as a function 
of the applied field, and the flame parameters (fuel, flowrate, burner type).  The PMT data 
is also extracted to evaluate flame luminosity oscillations.  Image data is processed using 
the OMA software (also developed and used by CLD Flame researchers).   
 
The overall data volume is large with a storage limit of 127,000 MB per test day.  All of 
the data has been downloaded to the hard drive with a backup system at UC Irvine.  At 
this stage, the data has been sorted into appropriate segments so that comparisons can 
be made between burner geometries (jet versus coflow from the prior round of testing), 
fuel type and dilution (methane versus ethylene; no dilution, modest dilution, high 
dilution) and fuel flow velocity.  The fuel flow velocity and dilution conditions were 
sometimes selected to hold total carbon flux into the flame constant.  At this stage, the 
analysis remains comparative and qualitative, to show the major differences in behavior 
in microgravity and normal-gravity (1-g) flames, and to show particularly how buoyancy 
modifies the electrical response of the flames. 
 
E. Preliminary Research Findings

metadata.source: 22 ACME E-FIELD Flames/Reports/E-FIELD Flames Final Report.pdf
metadata.relative_path: 22 ACME E-FIELD Flames/Reports/E-FIELD Flames Final Report.pdf

text:
in microgravity and normal-gravity (1-g) flames, and to show particularly how buoyancy 
modifies the electrical response of the flames. 
 
E. Preliminary Research Findings 
Distinctly different results were seen in E-FIELD Flames’ second round tests with the gas-
jet burner when compared with the first round tests with the coflow burner.  For example, 
the ion current response to the electric field strength with an upward ion driven wind in 
microgravity is a clear parabolic trend (which is similar to the trend observed in 1-g flames 
with the coflow burner as presented in the prior report).  The parabolic behavior is evident 
even with the strong oscillations observed during the rise.  This rising trend is not 
observed with the coflow burner.   
 
The behavior of the soot and its charge state are complicated since in the regions of high 
field strength, particularly near the fuel tube where the field lines converge, soot can emit 
or collect free charges.  Hence, the soot transport is driven directly by the field and by the 
ion-driven wind (and thermophoresis) which means it can travel differentially to the bulk 
flow.  These various transport elements can push the soot through the flame to burnout, 
hold it in stasis in the flame for additional growth, or drive it to the burner where it 
accumulates.  More work is needed to sort through these elements. 
 
Positive electric field for 100% methane fuel with jet burner  
The preliminary findings for the gas-jet burner in this section highlight the representative 
information of electric fields applied to a small hydrocarbon flame in the 0-g condition.  
The ISS tests covered a wide range of conditions which allowed the flame to settle as its

flame images representative of the jet tests conducted with methane as fuel.  The voltage 
is indicated as the nominal field strength (kV/cm).  Since the physical spacing from the 
burner to the mesh is 35 mm, 1.16 kV/cm represents nominal potential of around 4000 V

The very first image of each condition, e.g., at 0.05 kV/cm, demonstrates the initial 
voltage stage before the voltage sweep test commences.  The jet flames are relatively 
more stable initially and less stable under high voltage than the previously reported 
flames using a coflow burner with no coflow [Chien et al., Ion Current and Flame Changes 
with Electric Fields in Microgravity, WSSCI Pasadena 2019].  As the positive field is applied 
to the jet, the flame becomes both narrower and shorter.  An immediate change is the 
appearance of bright soot at the flame tip.  With an increase of electric field strength, the 
soot region diminishes as the flame shrinks.

slightly around the current peak and lifts higher, with one side of the reaction wing 
attached to the tube, as the electric field increases further.  The flame is not always lifted

dancing phenomenon can be seen from the i-v curve where the ion current oscillates

to 4 A) and reaching 4.0 A; corresponding flame images are shown as 1.86 and 2.16

discharge event.  The combustion extinguishes with the oscillations at 1.95 kV/cm for 24 
cm/s and 2.16 kV/cm for 19 cm/s.

In all of the i-v curves, the ion current data points at each field strength stretch across 
~0.1 A for each step, which are the jagged features from the spikes following a voltage 
step change that are mostly associated with the transient capacitance of the system when 
a rapid voltage step is requested.  These overshoots notwithstanding, the i-v curves follow 
smooth and reproducible trajectories. The wide range of the ion current after the 
saturation plateau is due instead to the flame oscillation.  
 
This report shows the initial results of the E-FIELD Flames experiment using the gas-jet 
burner in the International Space Station (ISS).  The positive field allows the soot to 
concentrate and compresses the flame into a high current density thermal source.  The 
flames demonstrate an unpredicted oscillation before extinguishing with increasing field 
strength.  This oscillating phenomenon was not observed during the tests with the coflow 
burner from the first round, with the exception of a case that introduced the airflow at 
30 cm/s which increased the surface reaction while the flame tended to balance between 
electric field effects, ions, and charged soot. The negative field allows the flame to 
maintain its spherical characteristic in microgravity. The yellow soot appears for both of 
the electric field directions within the flame around the tip and disappears with increasing 
field strength after reaching the current peak.  The role of soot in the i-v behavior of these 
flames requires further investigation.

2 featuring the 2.1-mm gas-jet burner) 
Week 02: March 2-8 
Nemo: Excellent job replacing the imaging module in the CIR HiBMS Imaging Package on GMT 064! Thank 
you for all your hard work and diligence during the many intricate tasks. You replaced this imaging module 
in support of the next ACME experiment, E-FIELD Flames (Electric-Field Effects on Laminar Diffusion 
Flames). 
 
Maker: Great job installing the ACME Mesh and replacing the ACME Bypass Controller on GMT 067! Thank 
you for all your hard work and attention to detail. You performed these tasks in support of the next ACME 
experiment, E-FIELD Flames (Electric-Field Effects on Laminar Diffusion Flames). 
 
E-FIELD Flames studies how electric fields at different voltages influence flames. An electric field can 
strongly influence the motion of the ions produced by a combustion reaction. The resulting ion-driven 
wind impacts flame stability and soot production and reduces pollutant emissions. The results will lead to 
a better understanding of more efficient and less polluting combustion technology for use on Earth. 
 
Week 03: March 9-15

metadata.source: 22 ACME E-FIELD Flames/Reports/E-FIELD Flames Final Report.pdf
metadata.relative_path: 22 ACME E-FIELD Flames/Reports/E-FIELD Flames Final Report.pdf

text:
wind impacts flame stability and soot production and reduces pollutant emissions. The results will lead to 
a better understanding of more efficient and less polluting combustion technology for use on Earth. 
 
Week 03: March 9-15 
On GMT 073, we performed the first ACME E-FIELD Flames (Electric-Field Effects on Laminar Diffusion 
Flames) test points. This first day was very successful with ten flames ignited for studying the effects of 
an electric field on laminar diffusion flames. Preliminary results show that the high-voltage electric field 
created forces similar to buoyancy, which dramatically affected the flame’s shape, intensity, and soot 
production. The ability to control flames with an electric field may have practical applications on Earth. 
For example, an electric field could be used to stabilize a flame in fuel-lean conditions, which would lead 
to reduced pollutant emissions compared to a typical combustor. 
CAPTION TO VIDEO, WHICH IS NOT INCLUDED IN THIS LOG 
While the light is still on at the beginning of this video, you can see the copper mesh, which is 
used to create the electric field. Before the electric field is activated, the flame is dim and 
spherical. However, as the negatively-charged copper mesh is energized at a steadily increasing 
potential, the flame becomes brighter and narrower—transforming into a shape similar to that of 
flames in normal gravity. The bright yellow tip is caused by soot. Near the end of the test, the

On GMT 078 and 080, we continued performing ACME E-FIELD Flames (Electric-Field Effects on Laminar 
Diffusion Flames) test points to study the effects of an electric field on laminar diffusion flames. All tests 
so far have used pure and nitrogen-diluted methane, the dominant component of natural gas. 
 
 
Figure 1. Composite Image of E-FIELD Flames at Increasingly Negative Electric-field Potential (100% 
Methane) 
 
Following ignition, the copper electrode mesh (downstream of the burner) is energized at a relatively low 
voltage and is then gradually stepped up to several kilovolts. In the current testing, the mesh is negatively 
charged relative to the burner. As a result, the electric field enhances the upward motion of the transient 
positive ions within the flame, inducing an “ion wind,” which affects the overall gas motion. 
 
Figure 1 shows how an increasingly negative electric-field potential affects a flame during a single test 
point. The resultant “ion wind” dramatically affects the flame’s shape, intensity, and soot production (the 
bright flame tip is caused by soot). This flame used 100% methane fuel; whereas, the tests conducted with 
40% methane were soot-free under all conditions tested. 
 
(Note that this is a preliminary image, where the apparent flame luminosity is not consistent from flame 
to flame.)

On GMT 095, we performed our first ACME E-FIELD Flames (Electric-Field Effects on Laminar Diffusion 
Flames) test points with a positively charged electrode mesh. These tests demonstrated the ability of the 
electric field to control the soot characteristics of a flame. We observed that the flames (30% ethylene) 
became soot-free at high electric-field potentials. While soot can be advantageous for some combustion 
processes, e.g., to enhance radiant heating, it is a health concern and often unwanted. Today’s tests 
demonstrated the potential for the practical application of electric fields to control soot within flames. 
One of the goals of E-FIELD Flames is to gain a fundamental understanding of this capability, which could 
lead to more efficient and less polluting combustion technology for use on Earth.

At the start of this test, before the positively charged electric field is activated, the top half of the 
flame is yellow because of the glowing soot. As the voltage is increased—ultimately to 10 
kilovolts—the soot fades away (so the flame is all blue), the flame shifts toward the burner, and 
the base dramatically broadens. The effect of the electric field on the flame can truly be seen 
when the electric field is deactivated near the end of the test, and the flame quickly returns to its 
natural state.

Figure 1. E-FIELD Flames with (left) and without (right) a Simultaneous Flow of Air 
(Flames actually dim blue; colored & brightened here for clarity) 
 
The “red” flame in Figure 1 benefited from the oxygen supplied by the simultaneous flow of air from the 
burner; in contrast, the “blue” flame relied on entrainment and diffusion for its oxygen supply. Although 
the fuel velocity is the same in both tests, the small “red” flame is attached to the burner, while the “blue” 
oxygen-starved flame is much wider and is lifted from the burner. These characteristics help the “blue” 
flame get the oxygen required to consume the fuel. Meanwhile, the “red” flame gets that oxygen in a 
much smaller zone thanks to the presence of the simultaneous flow of air. 
 
 
Figure 2. E-FIELD Flames at Increasing Fuel Velocity (No Simultaneous Flow of Air) 
(Flames actually dim blue; colored & brightened here for clarity) 
 
Figure 2 shows flames at increasing fuel velocities. Although the positive electric field tends to force the 
flames downward toward the burner, the flames are lifted from the burner because they are oxygen 
starved without the simultaneous flow of air. More oxygen is required to burn higher fuel flow rates, and 
the diameter at the base of the flame correspondingly increases. The distance that the flame is lifted from 
the burner also increases with the fuel velocity, where the separation allows more oxygen to reach the 
flame. The flame length is another measure of the oxygen transport, where the flame extends until it gets 
enough oxygen to consume all of the fuel.

with its yellow/orange top, stabilizes for several seconds. Then, the voltage is quickly increased to 
1 kilovolt. Under the influence of this electric field, you can see the flame broaden, turn all blue 
in color (i.e., become soot free), and become quite dim at the tip. When the electric field is 
deactivated just before the end of the test, the flame quickly returns to its initial condition—with 
its sooty top.

On GMT 117, the boot drive in the FCF Image Processor failed. As this hard drive stores all our science 
image data, we were unable to perform the planned ACME E-FIELD Flames (Electric-Field Effects on 
Laminar Diffusion Flames) test points. Next week, the crew will remove this hard drive, so we can boot up 
the FCF Image Processor from its other hard drive. Once this hard drive is ready to go as the new boot

ACME E-FIELD Flames Test Point Early Results 
 
Figure 1. E-FIELD Flames with and without a Simultaneous Flow of Air at Increasingly Negative Electric-
field Potential (100% Methane) 
 
Figure 1 shows how the flame changes as the potential of the negatively-charged electric field is increased. 
The top row of flames benefitted from the oxygen supplied by air flowing from the burner at the same 
time as the fuel. The bottom row of flames had no extra flow of air—only the oxygen in the air-like 
environment of the Combustion Chamber. In both cases, the effect of the electric field on the flame shape

text:
time as the fuel. The bottom row of flames had no extra flow of air—only the oxygen in the air-like 
environment of the Combustion Chamber. In both cases, the effect of the electric field on the flame shape 
and size is dramatic. The ion wind, an upward flow created by the negatively-charged electric field, 
enhances oxygen transport to the flame causing it to become narrower and shorter. 
 
The negatively-charged electric field also affects the ion current, or the electric current that passes 
through the flame due to the motion created by the ion wind. As the electric field continues to increase 
in strength, the ion current peaks then sharply drops to a lower ion current and the flame size increases 
correspondingly. In comparable testing in normal gravity, the ion current peaked at a lower current then 
plateaued instead of sharply dropping like the microgravity tests. Figure 2 below compares the 
microgravity tests with and without the simultaneous flow of air. The flames without the simultaneous 
flow of air peak at a lower ion current and at a lower field strength compared to flames with a 
simultaneous flow of air.

CAPTION TO VIDEO, WHICH IS NOT INCLUDED IN THIS LOG  
At the start of this test, the 100% ethylene flame is broad and bright with soot “horns.” These 
soot “horns” are caused by heavy soot production just within the flame. As the positively charged 
electric-field starts to strengthen, the flame starts to vigorously oscillate. You can see hot soot 
particles stream from the flame, where they would normally be consumed as they pass through 
the flame sheet. 
  
At about 3 kilovolts, the flame steadies and flattens because the positively charged electric-field 
tends to push the flame toward the burner. It appears that the soot is trapped within the flame 
by thermophoresis, in which the soot particles are driven from hot to cold. At about 8 kilovolts, 
the flame begins to pulse strongly in an axisymmetric fashion; whereas, the earlier oscillations 
were asymmetric. Finally, when the electric field is deactivated, the soot streams from the top of 
the flame.  
 
One of the goals of E-FIELD Flames is to gain a fundamental understanding of using electric fields 
to control soot production in flames. Results could ultimately lead to more efficient and less 
polluting combustion technology for use on Earth.

Due to a higher negatively charged electric-field strength, the right-hand flame in Figure 1 is lifted from 
the burner and tilts to the side. An electric field can strongly influence the motion of the ions produced 
by a combustion reaction. This ion motion affects the motion of neutral molecules, creating an ion wind. 
The overall result is similar to gravity’s buoyant effect on flames, where the hot gases are accelerated

text:
This test point video shows the strong effect of an electric field on an 80% ethylene flame. When 
the electric field is activated, the flame intensifies, and the soot, which causes the yellow flame 
color, gets brighter. As the field strength is increased, the flame becomes shorter and narrower. 
The flame then engulfs the burner outlet as the positively-charged electric field pushes the flame 
away. You can see sparks at the flame tip and later throughout the flame. The flame tip—in both 
position and soot intensity—oscillates at varying speeds, sometimes becoming steady for a 
moment. The flame continues to shrink in size until it basically encircles just the tip of the burner. 
You can see bright spots intermittently at the flame tip. At the highest voltages, soot periodically 
bursts toward the electrode mesh and arcing becomes visible at the mesh. When the electric field 
is deactivated, the flame gets bigger and dimmer until it goes out when the fuel is shut off.

text:
flames to be conducted in the Combustion Integration Rack (CIR), one of which being Electric-Field Effects 
on Laminar Diffusion Flames (E-FIELD Flames).  
 
In E-FIELD Flames, an electric field with voltages as high as 10,000 volts is established between the burner 
and a mesh electrode. The motion of the charged ions, which are naturally produced within the flame, are 
strongly affected by a high-voltage electric field. The resulting ion-driven wind can dramatically influence 
the stability and sooting behavior of the flame. Measurements are made of electric-field strength, the ion 
current passing through the flame, and flame characteristics such as the size, structure, temperature, 
soot, and stability. Conducting the tests in microgravity enables new understanding and the development 
of less polluting and more efficient combustion technology for use on Earth. 
 
This week marks the first week of E-FIELD flames operations with a very successful first set of ten flames 
ignited for studying the effects of an electric field on laminar diffusion flames. Preliminary results show 
that the high-voltage electric field created forces similar to buoyancy. This effect dramatically affected the 
flame’s shape, intensity, and soot production.

Appendix J. Summary of the ISS data collection 
The E-FIELD Flames data is all digital and includes both image and non-image data, where this is true for 
the other current ACME experiments.  To be clear, there is no collection of soot or other physical samples 
that are subsequently transported to the ground.  
 
The E-FIELD Flames image data includes images from the ACME DataCam, the CFI intensified camera (used 
with the CH* filter), and the High-Bitdepth Multispectral (HiBMs) camera (equipped with a red filter 
corresponding to the opposing CIR illumination package).  The DataCam images are in a Halcon Iconic 
Object (hobj) format, while the images from the CFI and HiBMs cameras are in a Tagged Image File (tif) 
format.  In contrast, the analog video was recorded on the ground in a Transport Stream (ts) format. 
 
The key non-imaging data from a test is a comma-delimited file that is described in detail in the Software 
Interface Design Description (ACME-DOC-010 Rev. D). 
 
The data is currently archived at NASA and work is underway to make it available publicly through NASA’s 
Physical Science Informatics System (PSI).

of both genders, and the general public.   His primary outreach focus is the fundamentals of 
microgravity (for which resources are available via  http://tinyurl.com/SEECmicrogravity) and human

National Aeronautics and Space Administration
Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME)
www.nasa.gov
advanced combustion via microgravity experiments 
Burning Rate Emulator (BRE)
• Objective: Fire Safety—To improve our fundamental understanding of materials ﬂammability, such 
   as extinction behavior and the conditions needed for sustained combustion, and to assess the 
   relevance of existing ﬂammability test methods for low- and partial-gravity environments.
• Flame/Burner: Flat perforated disk fed with gaseous fuel to simulate the burning of solid and 
   liquid fuels, where measurements are made of the thermal feedback upon which the vaporization 
   of such fuels depend.
• Investigators: Profs. James G. Quintiere and Peter B. Sunderland, University of Maryland; and 
   Dr. John L. deRis, FM Global (retired)
• Objective: Energy and Environment—To extend the range of ﬂame conditions that can be 
   accurately predicted by computational models, especially for highly dilute and heavily 
   sooting conditions.
• Flame/Burner: Coﬂow ﬂame where the gaseous fuel issues from an inner tube, which is centered 
   within a much larger outer tube, where an oxygen/nitrogen mixture issues from the annulus. 
• Investigators: Profs. Marshall B. Long and Mitchell D. Smooke, Yale University
Electric-Field Effects on Laminar Diffusion Flames (E-FIELD Flames)
• Objective: Energy and Environment—To gain an improved understanding of ion production in ﬂames 
   and investigate how an electric ﬁeld can be used to control ﬂames through the ion-driven wind.
• Flame/Burner: Gas-jet ﬂame, where (1) the gaseous fuel issues from a small circular tube into a 
   still atmosphere and (2) a high-voltage electric ﬁeld is established between the burner and a
